Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

[August 27th, 2025 6:44 AM] merili.randmaa: Vehicle verification feature state & concerns:

• Manual verification & cost
    ◦ there is reportedly a significant amount of human effort & cost involved in vehicle verification. Any launch should thus be first confirmed with Veritas team to prep resource allocation and agree on cost absorption
• Significant shortcomings in verification accuracy
    ◦ Only license plate is extracted and matched against admin selected vehicle
    ◦ Source of truth for admin vehicle data is largely unverified (i.e. based on unverified user input)
    ◦ Make/model/colour is not considered in verification
    ◦ Unsure if the condition of photo containing a vehicle is considered
    ◦ We have no data on failure rates and no understanding around false negatives/positives
• Enforcement & functionality
    ◦ Suspension logic is unusable - verification is tied to driver, not vehicle. Thus suspending based on verification result would cut out the driver recovery path
    ◦ Outside of suspension, there is no enforcement possibility - all failures currently still result in driver being able to go online, instead of enforcing a retry when for example a vehicle is not detected in the photo
    ◦ Only 4 wheeler vehicles are considered as eligible 
• Configurability
    ◦ Trigger signals are absent - we can not trigger based on vehicle changes etc
    ◦ We cannot configure it per category or per vehicle type
Thus, for example, the following scenarios are realistic:
• driver takes a photo of a tree, verification fails, but driver is still able to go online
• driver takes a photo of a random vehicle, verification fails, but driver is still able to go online
• driver attaches a license plate against a tree, verification passes and driver is able to go online
• driver writes a license plate number on a paper & tapes it to a car, verification passes and driver is able to go online
The above makes the vehicle verification feature ineffective in truly enforcing proper vehicle usage, at this point in time.

This feature was developed as a response to AZ government request and was done so in the bare-minimum MVP basis, just to show the gov that we have a feature.

As such, we recommend to pause further roll-out of this feature until it gets prioritised for maturing. We also recommend that this gets rolled back in PY, due to low tangible value and high potential risk of exposure of the feature's short-comings.

We have a hypothesis that a significant amount of incorrect vehicle usage instances are in fact caused by a lacking in-app functionality of forcing a driver to confirm the selected vehicle when they go online. If a driver has more than one vehicle on their profile, they might have simply forgot to change the vehicle they last used to the one they’re currently using :slightly_smiling_face:

When I was testing posterior-level aggregation, I found out that overall credible intervals are much tighter than previously.

I started researching and found out that this was because posteriors were tighter that variances generated by simulations (not because of aggregation).

The reason I see for this is that with simulations I was calculating a very pessimistic scenaro:

* I was sampling across different vmax-es, getting different errors
* The error is differently distributed across different vmaxes (e.g. can be higher as vmax increases)

[~accountid:618d2fe286c210006aa6241e], I reviewed the agreement and outlined high risk clauses below. Overall, these clauses are highly prescriptive and City-favourable. Key risks are:  

* *broad data ownership*; 
* *unlimited liability for data breaches*
* *data localisation and transfer limitations*; and
* *extensive operational disclosure of technical specifications*.

_13.1 - Service Provider Data Security Obligations_

(a) ‘Act only on the instructions of City’ - this effectively turns Bolt into a data processor of 'City data', but without a clear Data Processing Agreement framework. 

(d) and (e) Immediate notifications - Modify “_immediately notify_” to “_without undue delay, and in any case within 48 hours of confirmation_.”

* *What data do we expect to receive from or on behalf of the City under this Agreement? Did City share their DPA with us?* 

_13.2 - Data Ownership and Destruction_

City claims ownership of all data, including copies, summaries, and derivative works, which may include *Bolt’s operational data or analytics* derived from City data.

_13.4 - Data Security Incident_

13.4.2 requires the vendor to bear all costs of incident response, credit monitoring, PR, legal, etc., and *explicitly excludes liability caps* - this is a major red flag. We should limit cost-bearing to incidents caused by Bolt’s negligence or breach of contract.

_13.5 - Data Residency and Location_

This clause restricts *all primary data to remain within U.S. borders* which conflicts with Bolt’s data hosting infrastructure - we store user data in our AWS databases located in EU. Our current infrastructure cannot support this requirement. We must seek an exception here.

_13.6 - Access to City Network_

If Bolt accesses city technology assets then there are extremely detailed obligations for technical disclosure (architecture diagrams, APIs, bandwidth, etc.). This may require exposing confidential system design or proprietary IP. 

* *Will Bolt access any City technology assets?* If yes, then we should limit disclosures to information reasonably necessary for integration.

Thanks [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] 

* IMO, taking the Bolt Delivery approach (i.e., promoting exclusive offers of merchants/products that are being sold in Bolt app) is too risky here. The average complainant would interpret this as marketing for which consent is required, and so I think this could create a few headaches for us in the long term if we too readily allow it here.
* Otherwise, if I have interpreted your feedback correctly (apologies if not) it sounds like the team feedback is as follows - *Are we aligned on this*? (In particular, the suggested comms language under Item 1)

(cc. [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd]) 

----

{color:#4c9aff}*In short:*{color}

* *Phrasing*:
** We can consider rephrasing the comms (both the initial comms and the later comms) to focus on ‘Partner Offers’ as an app functionality. This approach is not without risk, but it lowers the likelihood that sending the comms without consent would create issues for us.
* *Mediums*:
** The approach we usually recommend for sending third-party marketing comms would be to rely on in-app banners and pop-up modals, as these are not ‘direct’ and so would not require consent.
** However, if the business wants to take a slightly riskier (but pragmatic) approach, we could consider sending these comms via push notifications (as it is unlikely that drivers would take issue with receiving these).
** Sending these comms via email (or in-app banners in inboxes) is the most risky medium for these comms.

Further details are below.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *_Are we able to word comms in such a manner that would still allow us to communicate over email & push (e.g. not naming offer providers directly, talking about it more as an app feature or part of the Bolt Rewards loyalty program ) to those with only promotional consent, but not specifically third-party consent?_*
{panel}

There is always the possibility that these comms will be interpreted as marketing that requires ‘partner offers’ consent, as a regulator may argue that the purpose of the comms is to encourage drivers to take up third-party offers. This is particularly risky in Poland, Romania and France, which are all ‘high risk’ countries from a marketing regulation POV.

Nevertheless, we can still lower the risk profile of these comms by minimising the likelihood that a regulator would interpret them as ‘third-party’ marketing (given that if we are marketing _Bolt_ products and services, it is unlikely we would need consent). To do this, the comms would need to {color:#36b37e}*only promote ‘Partner Offers’* {color}{color:#36b37e}*_as a functionality of the Bolt app_*{color} 💡 - i.e., as a place where exclusive bonuses, discounts and offers are available to Bolt drivers to give them additional value for the services that they need, rather than as a collection of third-party promotions. 

We would be happy to review the contents of the comms (when available) to bring them in line with the above - just let us know.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *_if the answer is no to the first question, can we use in-app channels such as pop-up modals and app inbox for the awareness comms?_*
{panel}

See above - We can explore reframing the comms to lower the risk profile.

* I would also flag that promoting third-party offers via _push notifications_ is lower risk (as this is less invasive and less likely to spark a user complaint, even though there technically is still a risk). As such, we could consider sending these comms without relying on ‘partner offers’ consent by {color:#36b37e}*limiting comms to push notifications, rather than emails*{color} 💡 

In any case, if we chose to de-risk things further by not relying on emails and push notifications at all, then we could promote third-party offers via the following mediums without relying on ‘partner offers’ consent 💡 (this is the approach usually recommended by our team for such comms, as such comms do not target specific drivers and so are unlikely to trigger consent requirements)

* {color:#36b37e}*In-app banners*{color}
* {color:#36b37e}*Pop-up modals*{color} (provided that this does not force the driver to consent to anything and can be easily closed)

As a final note, _in-app banners in inboxes_ have a similar risk profile to _emails_ in terms of sending third-party marketing, and so the above mediums would be preferred.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *_further down the line, we'd also like to communicate individual savings (e.g. you've saved X this month with Bolt Rewards / Offers) - would this be classified as a transactional comm if we only send this to drivers based on their activity? Or promotional? Or third-party marketing consent would still apply?_*
{panel}

As above, there will always be a risk that these comms are interpreted as marketing that requires driver consent - it is unlikely they would be classified as transactional (regardless of the phrasing). However, the risk of drivers actually complaining about these comms is lower, given that they are essentially telling drivers that they have saved money (which should be received positively).

Ultimately, we would make the {color:#36b37e}*same recommendations as above*{color} for these comms, in particular: (i) phrase them only promoting a functionality of the Bolt app; and (ii) limiting the comms to lower-risk mediums 💡 This would not eliminate the risk completely, but bring it down to a more acceptable level.

We have additionnal questions regarding the *launch format for two new tiered offers* that we plan to test within the *Branded Cars* program.

Until now, our plan was to structure the *tier levels* based on internal *profitability calculations* for the Branded Cars program, with fixed thresholds. Under this model, a driver’s variable branding remuneration would increase once they crossed a certain fix number of rides per month (e.g. 0–50, 50–100, 100–150, and 150+).

We would now like to *change this approach* and instead *link the tiered structure to Bolt Rewards levels*.

In practice, the driver’s remuneration would depend on their current Bolt Rewards status.

For example:

* Gold drivers → €100 fixed + €2 per ride
* Diamond drivers → €100 fixed + €4 per ride

*We would like your view on the following points:*

# Reclassification risk:
#* Could linking the Branded Cars offer to the Bolt Rewards loyalty program *increase the risk of reclassification* under French labour law, since it ties compensation more closely to the driver’s engagement level and performance on the platform?
# Dynamic nature of tiers:
#* Bolt Rewards levels are recalculated monthly based on driver activity and platform-wide performance. This means the thresholds change each month, and drivers cannot know in advance how many rides they need to reach the next level long-term.
→ Could this *lack of transparency or predictability* create a legal or contractual issue (e.g. regarding fairness, clarity, or misleading information)?
# 
# Contractual implications:
#* Would the Branded Cars Advertising Agreement or the Special Terms need to be updated each time a driver’s Bolt Rewards level changes?
#* Or could the contract simply refer to “the remuneration corresponding to the driver’s current Bolt Rewards tier,” without requiring monthly amendments?
# 
# VAT and qualification:
#* Since the tiered bonus would depend on Bolt Rewards status, would this in any way affect the classification of the payment as *advertising income (subject to 20% VAT)*, or could it risk being reinterpreted as a *performance or loyalty bonus* linked to transport activity?
# 
# Communication & compliance:
#* From a transparency standpoint, do we need to provide a minimum level of visibility or official notice to drivers about how their tiered bonus is calculated each month?
#* Would a monthly communication (email/push notification) outlining the updated conditions suffice to meet our legal and information obligations?



Thanks a lot for your help and insights on these points. 🙏 🙏 🙏

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

TL;DR
There are not so many profanity names we block and most of them are profanities indeed. In my opinion it doesn't make sense to invest time into fixing this issue unless the fix is really an easy one.

----------------
I checked our backend code that validates names for profanities and it appears we store them to the database table {{taxify_user.user_name_validation_pii_event}} already for quite a long time. So I queried how many names we didn't allow since the 01-01-2025:

* Only a first name is a profanity: 2258 times on 812 unique devices
* Only a last name is a profanity: 881 times on 414 unique devices
* Both first and last name are profanities: 3724 times on 1860 unique devices

So in total we blocked this year about 6.8k names on 3k unique devices{{Soso}} is the most popular profanity (used more than 1.5k times) in all three categories which is a short name for Joseph in Georgia, so maybe we should do something about it. Though using a full name won't be a profanity.{{Suck}} as a last name was used on one device 4 times this year, which is probably our user. On the other hand {{Suck}} that was used in different combinations of words that mean to be profanities was used 15 times on 13 unique [devices.In|http://devices.In] my opinion it doesn't make sense to invest much time into implementing a sophisticated solution with automated document verification. Language specific profanity dictionary can bring more harm than value as it's easy to abuse it. Maybe CS agents should be able to override the name validation after a manual document verification if from the legal point of view document exchange between a user and a CS agent is safe.

Hi Team,

Yes, in Azerbaijan, the rules are as follows: if a company is approved as a VAT-exempt by the government itself (mainly in sectors such as oil and gas, embassies, etc.), the government issues a special certificate to that company. The company then provides this certificate to all its vendors through the tax system.

Once the supplier receives this certificate, they issue all e-invoices to that company with 0% VAT, and in their tax report, they indicate that, based on certificate number X, an e-invoice has been submitted to this company without VAT. 

This refers only to the companies that have this certificate from the government. In all other cases even if the company is not a VAT payer, we issue VAT to them.

Please let me know if you have any questions.

Thanks!

Hey [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !

Legal view is that clause 2.1.3 is acceptable, but that 2.1.4 imposes high risks and *therefore should be previously assessed by DLA.*

Indeed, under Portuguese labour law, particularly as interpreted in reclassification jurisprudence, metrics that indirectly impose behavioral expectations on couriers (like individual acceptance rates) may be considered indicators of subordination, a key factor in recognizing an employment relationship.

If clause 2.1.4 imposes individual-level KPIs (i.e., acceptance rate per courier), even though it is formally doing it at a Fleet level, it still risks being interpreted as employer-like control, which could lead to reclassification claims, especially by ACT or Social Security authorities.

Maintaining performance thresholds at the Fleet level only (as reinforced by clause 2.3: _“shall not be applied towards individual providers of the Delivery Service”_) is a protective measure which aligns with the structure where the Fleet is the service provider and Bolt does not engage directly with individual couriers, preserving the contractor model.

However, we are happy to consult with DLA to confirm our view and will get back to you shortly.

In the meantime, we would visibility on how are you planning to implement this Fleet Agreements: are you planning to introduce this only to new fleets, or also to the already existing fleets? And in the second case, to all of them or only some of them? What is the criteria?

Thank you!

Good morning. As we progress with the investigation, I wanted to ask for your further help with understanding the impact on each market. I'll explain some useful context below to illustrate why we are looking for these details.

* *Law requirement:* DSA (EU law) requires us to display service provider information (contact details) to customers. Service providers = Fleets and Independent drivers. Fleet drivers are not service providers.
* *Business decision:* due to safety reasons (i.e. we do not want to expose driver data to riders), the business has decided to not comply with the DSA requirement above; however, such obligation still exists in the law.
* *Privacy issue:*
** *Issue in the EU:* Since we exposed not only service provider (fleet and independent driver) data, but fleet driver data, *for EU markets where fleet driver data was exposed, it can be qualified as a data breach* (pending further investigation)
** *Issue in non-EU:* DSA does not apply in non-EU markets, and so *for markets outside EU all exposure (fleet, independent driver, fleet driver) might* be considered as a data incident, but we need to understand the scope of drivers affected and their types. *Most important part from Privacy POV*: to determine the scope of the incident and to determine in which markets will it qualify as a data breach and assess whether we are required to report this incident under law.*This is why we require:*

Seems like the flakiness is related to the race condition among the tests according to the following scenario:

* Test {{Authorise and overcapture requests -> cancelled first authorisation and captured payment}} completes its execution but still has pending async operations, specifically:
** Fire-and-forget capture request to ProcessOut API with {{capture_amount: "20"}} 
* Test  {{Authorise with 0 amount and capture with actual amount requests -> captured payment}}) starts its execution flow and:
** Resets mocks to expect {{capture_amount: "10"}} (line 257 in test file)
** Receives the delayed capture request from the previous test with {{capture_amount: "20"}} instead

The fix is to let each test to complete its async operation by awaiting explicitly

Hi [~accountid:5acb1f48d8b95a2b34f150a8], the claimant has now responded with the attached email.

In short, she declined our offer of £105.78 and offers to *settle for £200* as full and final resolution if payment is made within 14 days. Failing that, she intends to proceed with the *Money Claim (£305.78).*

I think we have two realistic options here:

----

h3. *Option 1 – Accept the £200 Settlement Offer*

*Overview:*
Bolt accepts the claimant’s counter-offer of £200 “without admission of liability,” formally concluding the matter before court.

*Pros:*

* Resolves the claim quickly, with minimal further legal cost.
* The incremental cost (£94.22 above Bolt’s last offer) is less than the likely *legal time* required to defend the claim.
* Avoids a potential *small claims judgment* which could create *reputational risk* (especially if the claimant publicises the safety aspect).

----

h3. *Option 2 – Make a “Middle-Ground” Revised Offer (e.g., £150)*

*Overview:*
Offer a small uplift to demonstrate goodwill but avoid conceding to the full £200.

*Pros:*

* Maintains Bolt’s legal position while signalling compromise.
* Could be framed as “final without-admission goodwill offer.”

*Cons:*

* The claimant might still reject it, insisting on £200.

----

h2. Recommendation

I recommend *Option 1.*

While Bolt can technically defend the case, given the low claim value and safety narrative, a settlement is the most cost-effective path. The incremental £94 to accept her offer is likely less than Bolt’s internal cost to prepare and attend a small claims hearing.

Please let me know if you agree. If you do, I can send the claimant a Without Prejudice – Acceptance of Settlement letter confirming that Bolt denies liability and the payment is made as a goodwill gesture and in full and final settlement. I will also ensure the claimant agrees to withdraw the Money Claim upon receipt.

Please do let me know your thoughts on the above and let me know if you have any questions - thanks! 🙂

Hi [~accountid:62a057bc122dfd0069061724] - we have taken a look at this and our advice is below.

(i)  {color:#4c9aff}*In short:*{color}

* *Phrasing*:
** We can consider rephrasing the comms (both the initial comms and the later comms) to focus on ‘Partner Offers’ as an _app functionality_. This approach is not without risk, but it lowers the likelihood that sending the comms without consent would create issues for us.
* *Mediums*:
** The approach we usually recommend for sending third-party marketing comms would be to rely on in-app banners and pop-up modals, as these are not ‘direct’ and so would not require consent.
** However, if the business wants to take a slightly riskier (but still pragmatic) approach, we could also consider sending these comms via push notifications (as it is unlikely that drivers would take issue with receiving these).
** Sending these comms via email (or in-app banners in inboxes) is the most risky medium for these comms.

Further details are below. Happy to discuss if you have any questions 🙂 

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *_Are we able to word comms in such a manner that would still allow us to communicate over email & push (e.g. not naming offer providers directly, talking about it more as an app feature or part of the Bolt Rewards loyalty program ) to those with only promotional consent, but not specifically third-party consent?_*
{panel}

There is always the possibility that these comms will be interpreted as marketing that requires ‘partner offers’ consent, as the purpose of the comms is to encourage drivers to take up third-party offers. This is particularly risky in Poland, Romania and France, which are all ‘high risk’ countries from a marketing regulation POV.

Nevertheless, we can still lower the risk profile of these comms by minimising the likelihood that a regulator would interpret them as ‘+third-party+’ marketing (given that if we are marketing _Bolt_ products and services, it is unlikely we would need consent). To do this, the comms would need to {color:#36b37e}*only promote ‘Partner Offers’* {color}{color:#36b37e}*_as a functionality of the Bolt app_*{color} 💡 - i.e., as a place where exclusive bonuses, discounts and offers are available to Bolt drivers to give them additional value for the services that they need, rather than as a collection of third-party promotions. We would be happy to review the contents of the comms (when available) to bring them in line with the above - just let us know.

Additionally - as a general point - although the above proposal would allow us to promote partner offers in a way that is relatively low risk, there are higher-risk strategies available to the business. For example, another option would be to promote specific third-party bundle offers, but this carries a greater risk of regulatory escalation 💡 

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *_if the answer is no to the first question, can we use in-app channels such as pop-up modals and app inbox for the awareness comms?_*
{panel}

See above - We can explore reframing the comms to lower the risk profile.

* I would also flag that promoting third-party offers via _push notifications_ is lower risk (as this is less invasive and less likely to spark a user complaint, even though there technically is still a risk). As such, we could consider sending these comms without relying on ‘partner offers’ consent by {color:#36b37e}*limiting comms to push notifications, rather than emails*{color} 💡

In any case, if we chose to de-risk things further by not relying on emails and push notifications at all, then we could promote third-party offers via the following mediums without relying on ‘partner offers’ consent 💡 (this is the approach usually recommended by our team for such comms, as such comms do not target specific drivers and so are unlikely to trigger consent requirements)

* {color:#36b37e}*In-app banners*{color}
* {color:#36b37e}*Pop-up modals*{color} (provided that this does not force the driver to consent to anything and can be easily closed)

As a final note, _in-app banners in inboxes_ have a similar risk profile to _emails_ in terms of sending third-party marketing, and so the above mediums would be preferred.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *_further down the line, we'd also like to communicate individual savings (e.g. you've saved X this month with Bolt Rewards / Offers) - would this be classified as a transactional comm if we only send this to drivers based on their activity? Or promotional? Or third-party marketing consent would still apply?_*
{panel}

As above, there will always be a risk that these comms are interpreted as marketing that requires driver consent - it is unlikely they would be classified as transactional (regardless of the phrasing). However, the risk of drivers actually complaining about these comms is lower, given that they are essentially telling drivers that they have saved money (which should be received positively).

Ultimately, we would make the {color:#36b37e}*same recommendations as above*{color} for these comms, in particular: (i) phrase them only promoting a functionality of the Bolt app; and (ii) limiting the comms to lower-risk mediums 💡 This would not eliminate the risk completely (e.g., the comms would still count as marketing in any event), but bring it down to a more acceptable level.

* We know there’s a licensing requirement to have CCTV, and we know we don’t have it yet
* From privacy POV, we are supporting the team with the preparation for this
* Privacy requirements/safeguards will kick in when we will start offering the CCTV solution, not before we start doing it

+*UPDATE (05.11)*+

*Background*

* In the UK, it is possible that Bolt _might_ be considered an employer for pensions purposes.
** UK pensions regulator has opined that Bolt is an employer (however, we have not yet been served formal notice of it).
** This issue is limited to the UK for now. Ops believes that in the short term, no other countries will have pensions obligations (otherwise, we would have developed an in-house solution - see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1762334166192599?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]). 
* UK law states that employers must auto-enrol their workers into a pension scheme. As such, the current project involves implementing auto-enrolment.
** Currently, Bolt has an optional pension scheme with Aviva. 
*** In April last year (see [+LSS-32204+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-32204]), we launched pensions for drivers in the UK. T&Cs were prepared as an addendum to the Driver T&Cs ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OmWqQ9IIdayn-BAjAKH1B8CQYIP7q0hw/edit]). Per these T&Cs, enrolment was optional (drivers could opt-in via the app). Gab acknowledged that this was not currently covered in the privacy notice, but accepted the risk since it was opt-in. I cannot see evidence of a DSA, although this is likely because drivers were providing their data to Aviva directly.
** Main change is that this will now involve automatic enrolment.
*** Aviva will be moving Bolt drivers under the existing pension scheme to the new (auto-enrolment) scheme. The latter will be on less favourable terms, and Bolt will need to go through a consultation (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1762334166192599?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]).
** Plan is to onboard Zellis, which provides an online portal, payroll administration, payroll enquiries services, HR admin services, recruitment services, customer support etc.
*** Regional Legal has already reviewed Zellis T&Cs ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fPFoko6Ea8KdV38O45-n0wPRjxrXurkdkTSjEcozWw8/edit?tab=t.0]). One notable issue is liability capped at 12-month fees, and no obvious privacy indemnity.
*** It appears that the pension administrator will still be Aviva - Zellis is the administration expert acting as an intermediary between Bolt and Aviva (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1762334166192599?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]). 
** Drivers will still be able to opt-out of the pension scheme through Aviva (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1762334166192599?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]).
* Data sharing will be taking place under the proposed arrangement with Zellis.
** We will not be sharing any special category data or criminal records data, according to Ops (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09KXK4DV60/p1762334166192599?thread_ts=1762188941.452099&cid=C09KXK4DV60]). Ops is currently working on a full list of data categories that are being shared.
* Commercial negotiations with Zellis are still ongoing. I am waiting for a green light to commence formal review, which may be on 19 November.

*Privacy Issues / Action Items*

* NB. I struggle to see how ADM would apply here. Although enrolment is automatic, the decisions themselves are not - this is more characterised as an opt-out scheme. In any case, as this is the UK, our only concern here would be SCD due to legislative changes.
** Nevertheless, subject to further details, a *DPIA* may be helpful for this initiative ⚠️ 
* *Legal basis*: Currently unclear ⚠️ 
** This initiative will involve: (i) automatically enrolling drivers who have not currently opted for a pension provider, which will in turn mean sharing their data with the pension provider; and (ii) moving drivers under Aviva’s current scheme to the new scheme.
*** NB. Point (ii) is less of a concern for us from a privacy POV. Controller is the same, data and purposes are likely to be the same (it is Aviva doing the transfer, not Bolt). Question of whether this can be done is more a question for Regional Legal. As such, the more pertinent issue for us is the automatic enrolment (and data sharing) of drivers who do not currently have the pension set up.
** It is currently unclear what legal basis we can rely on to do so - if auto-enrolment is a legal obligation, then our lives are easier. If not, then we will need to consider either contractual necessity as the first port of call (if covered in T&Cs), then legitimate interest, and then (if the balancing test fails) consent as a last resort.
*** NB. We are not sharing any SCD / criminal data here, which makes things easier (but worth double-checking for Aviva) ✅ 
** In any case, it is good to hear that drivers can opt out of the pension. This is something.
* *Transparency*: Pensions are not mentioned in the privacy notice. As such, there is a transparency gap.
** This is particularly important here, as automatically enrolling drivers without their knowledge may feel intrusive and result in complaints if not properly handled.
** As discussed with Gab, best option overall would be *in-time notices*. 
*** This would guarantee that drivers are informed, would minimise divergence between existing driver privacy notices, and would minimise the risk of drivers from other countries viewing the UK privacy notice and incorrectly interpreting it to mean that drivers are considered employees generally.
*** I will therefore need to insert disclaimer language into whatever comms we will be sending, informing drivers that their data will be shared. This should include an overview of the purpose, legal basis (which will depend on whether legally mandatory), categories of personal data, and data recipient. Should otherwise include a link to the privacy notice ⚠️ 
** In the long term, we can consider updates to the privacy notice. However, for the reasons set out above (particularly as this is UK-specific), IMO it is not worthwhile doing so now.
* *Zellis Data Sharing*: Agreement needs to be amended ⚠️ 
** +Security+: InfoSec should review the security schedule to confirm that they are happy.
** +Subprocessors+: We should ensure more of a shift to specific, rather than general, authorisation.
** +Audits+: The agreement needs to contain an obligation on Zellis to allow for and contribute to audits (this is legally mandatory).
** +Costs+: The agreement currently states that DSSR/A32-36 assistance is at Bolt’s expense. We cannot accept this, as they are legally mandatory.
** +Notification Deadlines+: The agreement does not contain specific deadlines for Zellis to inform Bolt about DSRRs/PDBs.
** +Indemnities / Liability+: As advised by Legal already, we need a pro-Bolt privacy indemnity and a higher liability cap for Zellis.
* *Aviva Data Sharing*: If auto-enrolment of drivers who are not currently with Aviva means Bolt will be sharing the driver’s data with Aviva by default, we should really have a data sharing agreement in place with Aviva ⚠️ 
** I have not to date seen any such agreements - worth checking with Ops.
** If Aviva is a processor, then Bolt (as controller) may need to consider purpose compatibility and old scheme deletion rules in relation to any data migration to the new pension scheme. However, I imagine Aviva will be an independent controller - in which case,

** *Auto-enrolment*: The documentation / legal bases / mechanisms we need for this will depend on whether it is legally mandatory or not. Main issue here is drivers who are not yet enrolled with Aviva; those already involved should be fine from a privacy POV.
*** If it is, we should be ok. If it is not, we may need LIA/DPIA, as well as in-time option for drivers to opt out of sharing their data with Aviva in the first place (rather than retrospective opt out).
** *Transparency*: In any case, we should include in-time notices.

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Hi [~accountid:618bcc5c137a51006a5a95d6],

The issue falls mainly under *data protection and privacy compliance*, because the question is _what personal data about a driver_ (and under what lawful basis) Bolt can share with a third party (the fleet owner).

However, my view is as follows:

* Fraud-related cases usually involve personal data and sometimes allegations that could have reputational or legal consequences for the driver.
* Even if the fleet owner is the driver’s employer, *Bolt acts as an independent platform*, not as the employer’s agent. Sharing details about alleged “fraudulent behaviour” could therefore expose Bolt to risks under:
** *GDPR / data-protection law* – sharing personal data (including disciplinary outcomes) without a lawful basis or the driver’s consent.
** *Defamation risk* – if the information turns out to be inaccurate or not proven.

Please reach out to our Privacy team for a better advise.

Many thanks.

In my view, this agreement probably wouldn’t fully qualify as a barter agreement, since if Bolt allocates more “bonus” kWh to drivers in advance, Bolt might eventually need to compensate Stela financially for those kWh - just like any regular buyer would.

So, the part where Stela provides discounted EV charging in exchange for in-app visibility and promotion from Bolt should not be subject to additional payment.

However, if Bolt ends up exceeding the amount of “bonus” kWh and must pay for the extra usage, that portion would be treated as a normal purchase-sale transaction and taxed accordingly.

So, in short, a financial payment would only occur if Bolt exceeds the agreed “bonus” threshold and needs to settle the difference. Everything else would essentially be provided mutually free of charge.

The initial agreement is basically an improved and slightly modified version of the Bolt template — the core structure remains the same, so I don’t see any major risks here. From the data-sharing side, the privacy team has already approved both the main agreement and all annexes.

*Executive Summary*

Under German taxi law (§ 39 Abs. 3 and § 51 Abs. 5 PBefG), the decisive legal requirement is that the taxi operator receives the full tariff amount for each trip. The Bundesgerichtshof (BGH, I ZR 34/17 – Bonusaktion für Taxi App) confirmed that passenger-side discounts or subsidies are lawful as long as the driver’s income equals the tariff and the discount is financed by a third party, not by the driver.

In the proposed setup, however, the 5 percent “booking fee” would be deducted from the driver’s gross fare. That means the driver no longer receives the full tariffed amount, which risks being seen as an unlawful tariff undercutting.

To remain compliant, the 5 percent must be treated as a separate post-tariff commission (similar to the already existing commission) for mediation or technical services, not as part of the tariff calculation. The technical setup must show that the full tariff price remains intact and that any platform fee is independent of the tariff system.

*Detailed Legal Assessment*

The taxi tariff obligation under § 39 Abs. 3 and § 51 Abs. 5 PBefG is designed to protect the integrity of the taxi market. What matters is that the taxi operator receives the full tariff amount set by the local ordinance. The Bundesgerichtshof clarified this in the decision I ZR 34/17 (Bonusaktion für Taxi App). The court held that the tariff rule is only breached when the taxi operator’s actual economic inflow is below the tariff, meaning when the driver ends up receiving less than the amount prescribed by the tariff.

The source of the payment is irrelevant. It makes no difference whether the passenger pays entirely out of pocket, pays less because of a discount, or whether a third party, such as an app platform, contributes to or subsidises the fare. The key legal point is that the taxi operator must still receive the full tariff amount for each trip.

This is why promotional discounts and rider incentives funded by a platform are lawful. The BGH even said explicitly that it does not matter whether the passenger finances the fare “aus eigenen Mitteln oder aus Mitteln unabhängiger Dritter.” In other words, what the passenger sees or pays is not a tariff problem, provided the driver receives the full tariffed price.

Where things get critical is when the platform takes part of that tariffed amount back from the driver. If a 5 percent “booking fee” is deducted from the gross tariff before the driver receives payment, the driver is no longer getting the full tariff. That creates the appearance of an impermissible undercutting of the tariffed fare. Even if the total amount paid by the passenger remains at the official tariff level, the legal test focuses on what the driver actually receives.

So the compliant structure is straightforward. The driver’s fare and receipt must correspond exactly to the tariff amount. Any rider discounts, reinvestments, or demand-side incentives must be paid from the platform’s own funds, not recouped through a reduction in the tariffed payout.

If the plan is to add a 5 percent “booking fee”, it should be defined contractually as a post-tariff commission for mediation services, not as part of the tariff composition itself. The technical setup should make clear that the tariff remains untouched and that the booking fee is a separate commercial arrangement between driver and platform. That approach should keep the scheme compliant with the PBefG and consistent with the reasoning of the BGH.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Find alternative materials for hatch dampeners:

* Solid silicone
* EPDM
* Microcellural urethane

Best based on current search for us would be EPDM or Microcellural urethane because they have good spring back affect even when under pressure for longer period of time. Also they have good adhesive properties, so we can add adhesive on the dampeners like we are doing with current parts
Solid silicone based on performance is also good option, but silicone is difficult to glue therefor I would prefer EPDM or microcellural urethane.

In addition found that although EVA has good ‘'spring-back'' affect for shocks but not so good if there is a constant compression for longer time.
I our case foam pads under pressure for longer time and I found a test for this kind of application, ASTM D395.

ASTM D395 is a standardized test method that measures a material's ability to return to its original thickness after being held under constant compression for a long period, usually at a 
high temperature.

Common test time is 22 hours or 70 hours. Common test temperature is 70°C or 100°C

After the force is released, it is allowed to recover for 30 minutes. The "compression set" is the percentage of its original thickness that it fails to recover.
Then we can see that silicone and microcellural urethane recovers 85-95% of their shape, EPDM recover over 75% of its shape and EVA recover only 30% of it original shape.

Reviewed the Agreement with the city of Atlanta. Proposed changes and comments: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IDswuyZD1S4D5HqBm61yeTbp8xZPBhTdlc_9gdrsG9Q/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.5jgh45mtrt9h|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IDswuyZD1S4D5HqBm61yeTbp8xZPBhTdlc_9gdrsG9Q/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.5jgh45mtrt9h|smart-link] 

Key considerations:

# *Data Localisation (Clause 13.5)* 
## The draft requires all City Data to remain within U.S. borders, which conflicts with Bolt’s EU-based AWS infrastructure. There is no Georgia or U.S. legal requirement for data localisation - this appears to be a City-imposed condition. Bolt will push back with revised language allowing secure storage in EU data centres, supported by ISO-certified infrastructure and lawful transfer mechanisms (e.g., SCCs).
# *Undefined “City Data” (Clause 13.2)* 
## “City Data” is not defined, creating ambiguity around ownership and return/destruction obligations. Clarification is needed on whether this term includes only data provided by the City (e.g., parking zones, fleet caps) or also Bolt-generated data (e.g., trip and telemetry data). Bolt proposes to define City Data narrowly and retain ownership of its operational and anonymised datasets.
# *Processor Role & DPA Framework (Clause 13.1(a))* 
## The clause (“act only on the instructions of City”) effectively makes Bolt a data processor, but no Data Processing Agreement (DPA) framework is included. While not legally required under Georgia law, Bolt proposes to attach its standard DPA/DSA to clarify roles, scope, and data-handling obligations consistent with EU and international standards.
# *Incident Cost Liability (Clause 13.4.2)* 
## The draft obligates Bolt to bear all costs from any data breach - without limitation or fault threshold - and excludes the liability cap. This creates unlimited exposure, even for incidents outside Bolt’s control. Bolt’s revision ties cost responsibility to negligence or breach and restores the limitation of liability, aligning with commercial norms. 
# *Technical Disclosure Scope (Clauses 13.6.2–13.6.4)* 
## The current text could be interpreted to require detailed disclosure of Bolt’s system architecture and infrastructure. Revised language limits disclosure to high-level, functional details necessary for interoperability, protecting Bolt’s IP and trade secrets while maintaining transparency for integration and security.

    DATE(DATE_TRUNC('week', DATE(camp_ops.min_valid_treatment_period_start))) AS week_date,
    SUM(COALESCE(camp_ops.norm_gmv_eur,0) - COALESCE(camp_ops.norm_gmv_eur_c,0)) AS norm_delta_gmv_eur,
    SUM(CASE WHEN camp_ops.p_val_gmv_eur <= 0.05 THEN COALESCE(camp_ops.norm_gmv_eur,0) - COALESCE(camp_ops.norm_gmv_eur_c,0) END) AS norm_delta_gmv_eur_signif,
    SUM(COALESCE(camp_ops.norm_bonus_eur,0) - COALESCE(camp_ops.norm_bonus_eur_c,0)) AS norm_delta_bonus_eur,

    CASE 
      WHEN norm_delta_bonus_eur > 0 
        THEN norm_delta_gmv_eur_signif / norm_delta_bonus_eur
        END AS gmv_uc_ratio_signif

    -- norm_delta_gmv_eur / norm_delta_bonus_eur AS gmv_uc_ratio_signif
  FROM ng_public_spark.etl_campaign_operational_metrics_treatment_v2 AS camp_ops
  LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city AS sc
    ON camp_ops.city_id = sc.id
  WHERE 
    camp_ops.min_valid_treatment_period_start >= DATE('2025-10-06')
    AND camp_ops.min_valid_treatment_period_start < DATE('2025-11-03')
    AND camp_ops.treatment_period_type = 'discount'
    AND sc.name IN ('Paris', 'Johannesburg')

    -- AND camp_ops.p_val_gmv_eur <= 0.05
  GROUP BY 1,2,3
  ORDER BY 1,2,3{noformat}

[~accountid:5b7bbf35ed4f842a6ddb4648] queried battery data from the last 6 months for batteries where E13 had been triggered.[^E13_cell_data.csv] 

We found the average cell balance at each battery cycle and found that there is a pattern of how the batteries break. 
All batteries have normal cell imbalance (~10 mv) for most of the cycles. But at one point the imbalance starts rapidly rising. Investigation at Ilvestments will give us more information of any mechanical damage triggering this rise in cell imbalance. “One point” could be anywhere from 40 - 90 cycles.

One idea was to lower the E13 triggering condition from 80 mV → 50 mV, but the graph shows that we would catch batteries only 1-2 cycles before current trigger, also lowering the trigger level might great more false positives. 

Another idea was to find the rate of deltabalance change and see if it’s possible to catch faulty batteries with that. But as we see the delta balance rises very rapidly and batteries wouldn’t be caught much quicker.

We are now waiting for LG to inspect 3 batteries, ETA {{2025-11-14}}, to understand the scale of the LG cell quality issue.

I’d like to step in to provide a bit more context on this case. We received this deletion request some time ago and had already discussed it with the Fraud Team to understand why this account had been marked as “Fraud.”

The reason I instructed Ignacio to send the communication below and proceed with the deletion (which, as it turned out, was not technically possible from our side) was that, in practice, we do not fully delete this type of information. In reality, data related to such accounts remains in our systems and is not permanently erased. That approach has been discussed with the Senior Privacy Counsels, while the response to the requestor mentioned that we do indeed may retain certain types of data in our systems. Would not that ‘retained’ data be sufficient to prevent that individual from creating another account?

Only after sending the communication did we discover that we cannot change the account’s status from our end, despite having already confirmed to the requester that we would proceed with erasure. Therefore, I would like to explore the alternative/ exceptional solutions in this case. 

On a broader scale, we currently have two projects planned for 2026 that address retention periods for deleted accounts, as well as a global strategy for handling erasure requests concerning blocked or suspended accounts. As you can imagine, this remains an area with room for improvement, that we will put efforts into in the upcoming year.

Following up on the previous ticket regarding the MZM tenders, I wanted to share a quick update on the *Renfe Madrid* case (the first tender).

Renfe has expressed strong interest in MZM’s proposal and is now *moving forward in the administrative clarification phase* (“fase de subsanación”). In order to *fully accept MZM’s bid*, they have requested *non-binding supporting information* confirming that Bolt, as subcontractor, has the *capacity and experience* to provide the level of services required.

To clarify — Renfe is *not requesting us to sign or commit solvency*, but simply to *evidence (with figures)* that Bolt has historically operated at a service volume *above the minimum thresholds* required for this tender.

Specifically, the minimum requirements are:

* *Economic solvency:* Bolt Spain’s Annual turnover ≥ *€340,000*
* *Technical solvency:* Bolt’s Volume of executed services in a single year ≥ *€228,000*

We are *well above these figures* on an annual basis, so we can easily provide confirmation that these minimums have been achieved.

MZ's attached document and the accompanying draft declaration (“_Que la firma de esta declaración no implica compromiso alguno ni la existencia de un contrato formal entre las partes, ni la asunción de obligaciones económicas, operativas o legales por parte de Bolt._”) make clear that *this remains a purely declarative step*, with *no contractual or legal commitment* from Bolt.

*Next step requested from Legal:*
Please confirm whether we can provide this *declarative confirmation* of Bolt’s capacity, in line with the previous non-binding participation documentation. In case we want to proceed, we would need to sign this attached document and send them by 10th November at 10:00.

In this type of proceeding, the court issues a payment order (without a trial and without hearing the other party) based on the documents provided by the plaintiff, unless the claim is clearly unfounded or other conditions are not met. The defendant is entitled to file an objection, after which the payment order is no longer in force, and the court will hear the case in accordance with the general provisions.

Therefore we didn’t miss any correspondence and the court was not obliged to inform us about the proceeding before issuing the payment order.

*Drive | Automated Robocalls for Critical Overspeeding*

Hi everyone! We’re excited to announce that we’re rolling out automated robocalls for critical overspeeding cases!

*Problem*
Speeding is still one of the biggest drivers of vehicle damage and insurance costs across Drive. About *15% of GMV* goes into damage-related expenses, with speeding making up roughly *17%* of that.Today, handling critical overspeeding cases (40+ km/h over the limit in-city, 50+ km/h outside) is a *manual process* — CS agents reach out to users directly. While the team does a good job managing these situations, response times naturally vary based on workload and availability.This means that in many cases, it takes longer to reach users than ideal. Automating this process helps ensure immediate intervention in critical safety moments, keeping both drivers and vehicles safer.*Solution*
To address this, we’ve introduced *automated robocalls* that immediately contact users when critical overspeeding occurs.
When overspeeding is detected, the system:

# Sends a *push notification* and initiates a *robocall* to the user.
# If unanswered, a *second robocall* is triggered after 2 minutes.
# If still unanswered, the case is automatically *escalated to CS* for manual handling.

This automation ensures users receive immediate in-ride feedback and helps reduce the risk of damage or accidents.*Impact*
By reducing delays in intervention, we expect:

* Up to *0.33% GMV in cost savings* (repairs + MTPL)
* *Faster and more consistent response times* to critical overspeeding
* *Improved user awareness* and safer driving behavior

*Rollout*
The feature is LIVE across all markets (free-floating).*Thanks to everyone who made it happen*: ,

Upon further investigation, seems like the {{EaterMobileLaunchService}} logic is actually perfectly fine, but the pitfall is in [EaterWebLaunchService|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/platform/cs/support_webapp_gateway/main/service/eater_launch/EaterWebLaunchService.ts#L108] using [WebappUrlBuilder|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/common/customer_support/web_api/WebappUrlBuilder.ts#L289] which isn’t using [URLSearchParams|https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLSearchParams] (like {{EaterMobileLaunchService}} does) and it doesn’t therefore encode the params using {{application/x-www-form-urlencoded}} format (like [URLSearchParams.append |https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLSearchParams/append]does) - it doesn’t actually encode anything (!) so [WebappUrlBuilder|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/common/customer_support/web_api/WebappUrlBuilder.ts#L289] passes the initial message string encoded with {{encodeURIComponent}} causing it to be encoded yet before it arrives to {{/client/launchWebviewEater}} which then encodes it again.

The short term might be to decode the string in {{/client/launchWebviewEater}} but a long-term fix should be to get rid of that {{WebappUrlBuilder}} as it’s just prone to URL injection.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

On whether Article 588 ter M of Organic Law 13/2015 on Criminal Procedure" the same as "Criminal Procedure Act 2016 Article 588 (B)(V):

No, *they are not exactly the same article*, but they *refer to the same section of Spanish law* — the *Ley de Enjuiciamiento Criminal (Criminal Procedure Act)* — as *amended by Organic Law 13/2015*, which restructured that part of the law and introduced several new provisions, including *Article 588 ter M* and *Article 588 bis A to 588 sexies*.

Here’s how it works:

* The *Criminal Procedure Act 2016* reference you see in Bolt’s internal Spain table (Article 588 (B)(V)) is a *simplified reference* used in English translations. It refers to the same *block of articles (588 bis – 588 sexies)* added by *Organic Law 13/2015* that regulate *law enforcement access to data and the duty of cooperation of service providers*.
* *Article 588 ter M* is *one of those specific articles*, detailing the *obligation of service providers (like Bolt)* to cooperate with law enforcement in providing data relevant to a criminal investigation.

So in essence:

* *Both derive from the same legal reform (LO 13/2015)*;
* *Both regulate the same concept — cooperation with authorities during investigations*;
* The difference lies only in *how the article is cited* in various sources or translations.

✅ Therefore, for Bolt’s purposes, a request citing *Article 588 ter M LO 13/2015* is *equivalent in legal effect* to a request citing *Article 588 (B)(V) of the Criminal Procedure Act 2016* — and is *accepted* under our internal Spain guidance.

h2. *Outline of Preliminary Agreed Process With the Web Team:*

* *Regular Review of Cookiebot Declaration Page:*
** The Web Team will check the Cookiebot declaration page once per sprint (*every two weeks*) to identify newly added and unclassified cookies - such cookies can be added by other teams such as martech, growth, etc.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
* A *retroactive review instead of a proactive approval process* is intentionally adopted at the Web Team’s request, as *adding cookies and trackers promptly is business-critical* for marketing and analytics operations. Requiring prior approval for every new cookie would be unrealistic considering current web team’s resources and will create bottlenecks for both the business and the Web Team, delaying essential launches and campaigns.
* Given the *limited resources of the Web Team* and the dynamic nature of script additions through GTM, a retroactive process still allows to address compliance risks *without compromising business agility or operational feasibility*.
{panel}

* *Manual Classification:*
The Web Team will manually classify unclassified cookies following the [Cookie Consent Guidelines|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MW/pages/3648948262/Cookie+Consent+Guidelines]. 
* *Tracking via Jira Tickets:*
For each review cycle, the Web Team will create a Jira ticket with a defined prefix (e.g., “COOKIE–”) to track:
** Unclassified cookies pending clarification.
** Actions taken to resolve outstanding classifications.
* *Notifications of New Scripts:*
** Web Analyst ([tom.gander@bolt.eu|mailto:tom.gander@bolt.eu]) will notify the Web Team when new scripts or vendors are added through Google Tag Manager (GTM), prompting a review for potential new cookies.
* *Coordination with Other Teams:*
** The Web Team will liaise with the relevant subdomain owners (e.g., Chauffeur, Food, Fleet) to confirm the purpose of cookies originating from their implementations and update Cookiebot accordingly.
** The Web team will reach out to the Privacy Team in case any support needed with classifying cookies. h3. 1. *Summary of the request*

*Authority:* Swedish Police (Polismyndigheten)
*Date:* 30 October 2025
*Requested data:*

* Identity of the person who rented the vehicle
* Route and trip details
* Payment/account information
* Other rides made by the same account between 20 September and 10 October 2025

*Legal basis cited:* _10 kap. 2 § offentlighets- och sekretesslagen (OSL)_

----

h3. 2. *Verification against Bolt’s official policy*

Per Bolt’s *“LERs – Legal bases ACCEPTED by Bolt”* for Sweden, the following are recognised legal bases for disclosure:

* *The Swedish Code of Judicial Procedure (1942:740)* —
Chapter 23, 27, and 38 (preliminary investigation, seizure, and production of documentary evidence)
* *Public Access to Information and Secrecy Act (OSL) 10:24* —
Valid *only* if the data concerns a suspected crime punishable by imprisonment
* *Police Act (1984:387)* —
Section 25, in relation to transport operators, if the request concerns passenger data crossing borders

----

h3. 3. *Assessment of the cited legal basis*

The police cited *OSL 10:2*, which provides that confidentiality does not prevent data disclosure _between Swedish public authorities_ if it is necessary for one of them to perform its duties.

This clause:

* *Applies only to authority-to-authority disclosures*
* Does *not* impose obligations on *private companies* like Bolt
* Therefore does *not constitute a legal obligation* under *Article 6(1)(c) GDPR*

This is confirmed by the _“LERs – Legal bases NOT accepted by Bolt”_ list, which includes the *Public Access to Information and Secrecy Act (OSL)* but *only recognises Section 10:24* as acceptable for private-sector disclosures.

Thus, _OSL 10:2_ is not acceptable under either Bolt’s internal policy or Swedish law for processing personal data in response to law enforcement requests.

|*Authority*|Swedish Police (legitimate, @polisen.se domain)|
|*Requested data*|Trip, account, and payment data|
|*Legal basis cited*|OSL 10:2|
|*Acceptable basis?*|❌ No — applies only to inter-agency data sharing|
|*Correct basis (if resubmitted)*|OSL 10:24 (if the offence is punishable by imprisonment) or Chapter 23, 27, or 38 of the Swedish Code of Judicial Procedure|
|*Recommendation*|Reject request; ask police to reissue under a valid legal basis|

+*BACKGROUND*+

* In Romania, Bolt is collaborating with FATII (a third-party foundation that supports drivers by helping them with administrative, legal, and professional matters).
* Dataflows will be as follows:
** FATII will collect driver info (name, phone number, city) via their registration form (i.e., data sharing is one way: FATII → Bolt).
** FATII will then share these details with Bolt.
** Bolt’s M+ outsourced team will then contact the drivers (presumably by phone) to: (i) help them to register their self-employment form; and (ii) promote Pick’s services (a Bolt Rewards partner offering driver tools and benefits) to those drivers.
*** i.e., Bolt will be marketing third-party services to these drivers.
* Ticket with main agreement is here ([+LSS-58345+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-58345]), but currently empty (i.e., Legal is working on it).
* *Request*: Assess compliance and determine if a DSA is needed.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *Direct marketing*:
** Since Bolt is marketing the services of a third party, we require driver consent to be able to do this (this is particularly important in Romania, which is a high risk jurisdiction). Soft opt-in would not apply here.
*** Such consent must be specific and clear (i.e., not merely accepting T&Cs), particularly as this relates to drivers who clearly need assistance with legal matters. It should also be recorded in our systems accurately.
** A key question is whether these are existing Bolt drivers or new Bolt drivers:
*** Existing = Provided they have consented to partner offers, then we can send the comms.
*** New = We cannot end the comms until the drivers have consented. We would need to introduce a consent collection mechanism during this flow. This could be either: (a) during FATII’s registration flow; or (b) during the initial service comms with the driver.
** Another key question is what medium we will be using to promote Pick’s services.
*** If we are relying on email or text, we definitely need consent.
*** If live calls only, DM rules do not apply (automated calls would be caught, but human operators are fine). It appears that telemarketing in this way does not explicitly require opt-in consent.
** The usual opt-out rules also apply here. We must ensure we have an efficient means of actioning and tracking this.
* *Data sharing*:
** FATII is unlikely to be collecting the driver data in the first place on Bolt’s behalf. As such, this is likely a controller-to-controller relationship.
*** As such, we need data sharing provisions. Since Bolt is only the _recipient_ of the data here, I see little value in implementing the full DSA (which would place the bulk of obligations on Bolt as the data importer). Instead, short form provisions should suffice - I have prepared these here ([{color:#ff5630}+*LINK*+{color}|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PmwPB8tqD8a-7yZSWEUdx1uXAj86pLWM2fO4MKoH1_s/edit?tab=t.0]).
** Main concern is ensuring that FATII has an appropriate legal basis for sharing driver data with Bolt (and that FATII has been sufficiently transparent, as drivers may think they are just dealing with FATII), so that we will not be blocked by complaints.
*** FATII sharing contact information with Bolt for service assistance AND marketing is two different purposes. We want to take steps to minimise Bolt liability for any ‘purpose creep’.
** Data sharing is within the EU, so no need for SCCs.
* *Other*:
** Overall, the data sharing element is low risk. The more important element is marketing.
** Both forms of contact with drivers (operational comms and marketing) are covered in the driver privacy notice. Likely legitimate interest and consent as the applicable legal bases.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Presumably FATII is not registering drivers at Bolt’s request here, and has its own purposes in tandem?
** Are these drivers Bolt drivers already, or have they not yet signed up for Bolt when FATII passes over their details?
** How will we be contacting drivers - specifically to send them Pick marketing - emails / texts / live calls?
** Will we be doing any data sharing with Pick?
* Advice:
** Marketing:
*** Depending on how we are contacting drivers, we may need their opt-in consent to do so.
*** How we collect such consent will depend on whether the drivers are current or prospective drivers.
*** In any case, we should ensure that opt-out mechanisms are in place that are enforceable, and that we identify ourselves in the comms.
** Data Sharing:
*** We should include these provisions ([{color:#ff5630}+*LINK*+{color}|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PmwPB8tqD8a-7yZSWEUdx1uXAj86pLWM2fO4MKoH1_s/edit?tab=t.0]) in the main agreement.

The legal basis cited is the *“Loi de financement de la Sécurité Sociale 2008”*, which extends the _right of communication_ granted to agents of social security organisations under *Articles L.114-19 and L.114-20 of the French Social Security Code*.

----

h3. 2. Overview of the request

* *Requesting authority:* _Caisse d’Allocations Familiales du Nord – Service contrôle allocataire_ (Social Security authority).
* *Purpose:* Financial control of a welfare beneficiary’s situation (verification of income).
* *Data requested:*
** Earnings from Bolt (professional activity income).
** Information on Bolt’s handling of expired residence permits (platform compliance process).
* *Legal basis cited:* Law of financing of the Social Security 2008, referring to _Articles L.114-19 and L.114-20_ of the _Code de la Sécurité Sociale_.

----

----

h3. 1. Scope and intent of the cited provisions

Articles *L.114-19 and L.114-20 CSS* grant a _“droit de communication”_ to *agents of social-security bodies* (such as CAF) for the purposes of:

* verifying the accuracy of beneficiaries’ declarations, and
* recovering benefits unduly paid.

This right allows those agents to obtain _“documents et informations nécessaires”_ *from persons or entities having professional relations with the beneficiary*, without professional-secrecy objections.
Failure to comply may trigger an *administrative fine* (1 500 € per insured person, capped at 10 000 €).

----

h3. 2. Applicability to Bolt

CAF’s request clearly relies on this right of communication.
However, the text refers to _“personnes physiques ou morales qui entretiennent ou ont entretenu des relations professionnelles avec la personne contrôlée.”_
This usually targets:

* *employers*,
* *banks*,
* *telecom operators*,
* *energy providers*, etc.

In practice, private digital platforms such as Bolt *do fall within that broad category*, since they have a contractual relationship with the individual.
Therefore, *CAF’s right of communication* *_does_* *formally extend to Bolt*.

----

h3. 3. Compatibility with the GDPR

Under *Article 6(1)(c) GDPR*, processing is lawful if it is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation _to which the controller is subject_.
Here:

* Articles L.114-19 and L.114-20 CSS expressly impose an obligation to communicate documents “dans les trente jours”, and
* failure to do so is sanctioned.

Hence, *this constitutes a genuine legal obligation under French law*, meeting Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.
CNIL has also acknowledged that communications made under the _droit de communication_ fall within lawful processing based on a legal obligation.

----

h3. 4. Data-minimisation considerations

Even if the legal basis is valid, the *scope must remain proportionate*:

* Only data *necessary to verify Mr El Yebadri’s professional income* should be disclosed (for instance, aggregated earnings per month).
* The second question (“does Bolt block workers when the residence permit expires?”) concerns *platform policy*, not personal data, and is *not required* to verify income — it may therefore be declined.

----

----

Concerning the work permit >< blocking on app question:

h3. 1. What CAF is asking

CAF is *not* asking for any personal data (not the driver’s permit status), but rather:

{quote}_“Pouvez-vous m’indiquer également si l’application bloque les travailleurs si leur titre de séjour n’est plus valable ?”_{quote}

So, this is a *general operational question* about Bolt’s compliance system — how the app functions when a work authorisation expires. It is a _process_ query, not about Mr El Yebadri himself.

----

h3. 2. Does Article L.114-19 CSS cover this kind of information?

No.
The _droit de communication_ applies to *documents and information necessary for checking the sincerity of a beneficiary’s declarations or recovering undue benefits.*
While it gives CAF broad access to data about the _individual beneficiary_, it does *not authorise requiring a private company to describe or justify its internal operational rules or compliance systems.*

In French administrative practice, the “informations nécessaires” refer to *facts and data directly connected to the beneficiary’s situation* (e.g. income amounts, employment periods, invoices, etc.), not to general company processes.

----

h3. 3. GDPR implications

Even if the question does not involve personal data, responding would mean *disclosing internal operational details* about Bolt’s platform. That is:

* not _required_ by law;
* not _necessary_ for the control of the beneficiary’s benefits; and
* potentially sensitive from a *security and compliance perspective* (as it concerns account-blocking mechanisms).

Under *Article 5(1)(c)* GDPR (data minimisation) and *Article 6(1)(c)*, only information necessary to comply with the specific legal obligation should be shared.

----

h3. 4. Recommended stance

* ✅ Share *the income information* (since it is directly relevant and covered by L.114-19 CSS).
* ❌ Decline to describe Bolt’s internal controls, as this is outside the scope of the _droit de communication_ and not required to verify the beneficiary’s situation.

Hi [~accountid:712020:02e8ad5d-a35d-44b9-b445-6111cdb230dc] this is exactly what I mentioned - exchange of services is a barter. I will try to explain it again:

A barter is when two parties exchange goods or services directly, _without using money_ as payment.
Example:

* A marketing consultant designs a logo for a fitness studio.
* Instead of paying cash, the fitness studio gives the consultant free gym pass for a quarter.

Both sides receive something of value, but no cash changes hands.

Even though no money is exchanged, *barter is still considered a transaction* because:

* Each side *supplies* something.
* Each side *receives* something of measurable value in return.
* For VAT purposes, each supply is *treated as if sold for its market value*.

So in practice, both parties:

* Issue invoices (often showing the same value).
* Account for VAT (if applicable) as if they had sold and bought something for money.
