Thanks [~accountid:625fd5780f5cf500697eb894] - this is helpful. I include my preliminary thoughts below, together with some follow-up questions. 

{color:#4c9aff}*In short*{color}:

* We should include some data sharing provisions in the commercial contact that we use with FATII.
* Depending on _how_ we will promote Pick’s services to drivers, we need to be careful about making sure that the driver has already consented to receiving third-party marketing.

----

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS*
{panel}

# Regarding the drivers that FATII is registering via its registration form - Are these drivers exiting Bolt drivers, or are they in the process of signing up to Bolt?
# Presumably FATII is not solely registering drivers (via its registration form) at Bolt’s request, but instead has its own purposes for doing so?
# What mediums will we be using (e.g., emails, text message, live phone calls) to promote Pick to the drivers?
# Will this arrangement involve any personal data sharing with Pick?

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*PRELIMINARY THOUGHTS*
{panel}

*Legal Framework / Contracts:*

* Since Bolt is only _receiving_ personal data here (and not _sending_ it to FATII), we do not need a full Data Sharing Agreement here. 
* However, to ensure that our position is protected in relation to any data that FATII sends us (e.g., we want to be protected in case FATII has collected any of this data without a proper legal basis), we should include some ‘light touch’ data sharing provisions in the commercial contract that we enter with FATII. 
** I have prepared the clauses here: [{color:#ff5630}+*LINK*+{color}|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PmwPB8tqD8a-7yZSWEUdx1uXAj86pLWM2fO4MKoH1_s/edit?tab=t.0]. I have notified the Legal Team on [+LSS-58345+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-58345] to include these clauses in the main agreement ✅ 

*Marketing Pick to Drivers:*

* The main risk here concerns {color:#ff5630}*whether and how we collect the driver’s consent*{color} to receiving promotional comms about Pick ⚠️ 
** As we will be promoting the services of a third party to the drivers, we may be required to first collect the driver’s consent in order to do so.
*** Whether we will be required to do so will depend on the medium that we are using to promote Pick’s services - if we are using email / SMS texts / automated calls, then consent will be required; if we are only promoting Pick over the phone / live calls, then we can proceed without consent.
** If we are required to collect consent (i.e., we use emails / SMS texts / automated calls), then we must made sure that we have this _before_ we promote Pick’s services to the drivers. There are multiple ways that we could collect this, depending on whether the drivers are _existing_ Bolt drivers or _in the process of signing up_:
*** +Existing Bolt drivers+: If the driver has consented to ‘partner offers’ in their Bolt app, then we have already collected their consent and so can proceed with promoting Pick to them 💡 
*** +Prospective Bolt drivers+: These drivers will not yet have consented to ‘partner offers’ in the app, and so we need to be careful about how we collect consent here. We can consider the following options, depending on the setup with FATII 💡 
**** *Option A*: We explore whether, as part of FATII’s registration form, they could include a separate checkbox in which the driver consents to Bolt contacting them about third-party promotions. I would not necessarily recommend this as it raises operational challenges (i.e., FATII would need to have a system for sharing these consents with us), but flagging it for completeness.
**** *Option B*: During the initial (service-related) comms with the driver to help them with registering their self-employment form, we can ask for the driver’s consent to receive parter offers / third-party marketing (if such comms are over the phone, we can ask them to verbally consent and then make a record of it on our systems).
* In any case, we must also ensure that the drivers at all times have a clear means of opting-out of receiving promotional comms about Pick 💡 

Happy to discuss if you have any questions 🙂

We checked the vehicle logs with [~accountid:712020:7636318d-11ba-448e-8ae7-b935370c0640] & [~accountid:6215e9f275803500683497d5]. 

From logs, it seems like 697-767 was the main culprit behind the incident, it was a C1 battery ([DSB2101220290|http://prelive-iot.internal/westeu/iot/?scooter=2aa1710c&from_ts=1762401836&to_ts=1762409444&full=1]) with no prior cell errors hinting of any issues. The battery first started to heat up, increasing from the ambient ~20 degrees temp. up to 32 degrees in 4 minutes (fixed at 05:57:23 UTC), and at 06:01:41 the logs recorded a BMS temperature of 87 degrees. From this point on, there are a lot of BMS related errors & cell voltage readouts with varying cell values for single cell groups, highlighting that something is badly wrong with the battery. *There were no prior errors pointing towards the BMS failing*. It had been used on field at Lisbon since 4th August 2025 (2 months) straight without any BMS-related errors until the fire.

!image-20251106-123221.png|width=1014,alt="image-20251106-123221.png"!

Second battery ([DSM2203050131|http://prelive-iot.internal/westeu/iot/?scooter=2ad8dcd9&from_ts=1762403328&to_ts=1762410348&full=1]) from 183-400 presented steadily growing higher temperatures & cell error only after the first battery internal temperature had rised to >100 degrees, leading us to believe that this fire was a byproduct of the first battery burning.

Nothing else to remark before we see the full video/report from LOPS.

[~accountid:712020:08936576-e6a0-4b43-900f-6ddfe34f6c67] thank you for raising this ticket. I do understand that similar Code of Conduct is common practice all over markets. However having reviewed this Code, I do not recommend to sign it:

* *“Strictest requirement” override.* If law and the Code differ, we must follow the strictest rule-turning soft guidance into hard obligations everywhere we operate.
* *Unrestricted audit rights.* FSN (or its auditor) can come “at any time” with *unlimited* access to premises, documents, and employee interviews—over-broad vs. confidentiality and data-protection constraints. This is a hard no from Bolts side.
* *Control over subcontracting + full tier disclosure.* Prior consent to outsource and duty to reveal *all* sub-suppliers (including contacts) for inspection—commercially intrusive and impractical. 
* *Subjective reputation veto.* We must avoid activities that, *even if lawful*, could “harm” FSN’s reputation—an open-ended termination lever.
* *Over-broad ESG due diligence duties.* Annual environmental risk assessments at *every* facility and due-diligence across the *entire* supply chain go beyond a proportionate, risk-based approach.

What is the value of the initial agreement? Thanks.

Hi Silja,

There are several pages dedicated to managers in [Manager’s Playbook giving overview of our equity compensation|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/BMP/pages/4427186625/Equity+Compensation], how it works and what principles we have in place, guides, etc. No less important is the general [Bolt’s Option Program page|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/BILP/pages/3748954176/Bolt+s+Option+Program] that is accessible to all employees.

Equity compensation is set as a % of annual salary. For each compensation grade we have equity range in place (as mentioned in % format) and this works on top of someones individual cash compensation. So if to want to compare team members then starting point would be to see whether for all equity ranges are followed. However, it should not be a goal itself that all team members must have exactly the same amount of units and/or valuation in place, as this could only work if they all joined at the same time, to the same roles, with exactly the same compensation, have all exactly the same amount of issued equity previously, have been promoted or changed jobs exactly in the same pace and same details, etc, and this is very unlikely. Additionally, while equity ranges give guidance on how much team members in specific roles should have equity compensation, the end result is heavily dependant on their performance.

Managers have the possibility to review their whole team total compensation (i.e. cash and equity) holistically during ACR. Outside of ACR equity can additionally be awarded in case someone fully vests their initial grant, making them eligible for a [refresh grant|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/x/YIAhWAE], or if person is promoted.

[~accountid:5e0f07ab9a4b780d990e9fb9] here is the general approach:

# When responding to those kind of letters from the Czech Trade Authority we should try to prove that the damage was caused by the consumer. This means that we should provide the report and explain, in particular:
a. how the telematics data shows that the damage happened during the consumer’s rental period, under circumstances indicating their fault (for example, a strong impact or collision event),
b. why these findings exclude other possible causes,
c. and refer to the relevant provisions of the T&C that define the consumer’s liability.
# The smaller the case, the less detailed evidence we should provide, to avoid unnecessary workload for the team.
# If, after reviewing the case, you believe that the damage may not have been caused by the consumer, we can simply accept the claim.
# If we decide to respond to the letter and the Czech Trade Authority does not agree with our position, we can propose a settlement.
# As for the fines: we must provide additional proof to justify the calculation of the damage when claiming damages that exceed the fines specified in the T&C. Also, fines stated in the T&C should be proportionate to the actual damage in a given case – consumers should not be charged excessively high penalties.

Therefore please prepare a response accordingly (unless you decide to accept the claim – point 3). Once the response is prepared, please attach it here for review. Let me know in case of any questions.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Since the installation of cameras is the responsibility of the dispatch centre, it is the dispatch centre, not the drivers or fleet, that bears liability. Therefore, any warnings from the authorities should be directed to us. 

Based on our understanding, Danish authorities usually start with a warning in cases of non-compliance, rather than imposing immediate hard restrictions. If the issue isn’t resolved within the given timeframe, they may proceed with stronger enforcement measures such as fines and ultimately suspension of license. However, given the nature of this in-compliance (which could interfere with ongoing and urgent police investigations), we should be aware that timeframes for rectifications can be short or very short. 

Since we already have a plan to resolve the issue and the policy team is aware, these are strong indicators to show the road authorities that we’re taking corrective action - which should help mitigate the risk of fines or restrictions.

Given the above - we need to be cautious in communicating to the FOs at this stage. Anything we say can reach the attention of the authorities, and if there is a misconception that this lies on the drivers, then they can use any communication to exculpate themselves visavi authorities. It would be strongly advisable to wait with communication till we have a compliant solution in place, and even then, any communication needs to be drafted in a way that we do not admit to any previous non compliance. Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*_BLOCKING_*
{panel}

It, of course, depends on the user type (driver, courier, rider, eater) and the “block” length (i.e. if it’s a temporary suspension or a permanent block). 

* Automated blocks are usually considered high risk from privacy POV, as the law (and the privacy regulator in the EU) considers permanent blocks to have a significant effect on the user (all types, but drivers and couriers have heightened risks).
* That’s why [~accountid:624d3e6b699649006aea9c98] and [~accountid:62722e092db308007024a425] have been working on the Blocking project - mapping out reasons, preparing transparency bits (messaging) etc, and more importantly - working on the human review mechanism.
* I suggest liaising with them to ensure that this blocking logic follows the process we have, to ensure that we’re not assuming any unnecessary risks.

✅ What I suggest doing, after aligning, is to implement human review in all these cases. In practice, if we, say, suspended the user temporarily, a human would need to review and document that decision in line with the process we have. This way, we would minimize the risks to the extent possible when it comes to automated decision-making (and perhaps other elements outside privacy scope).

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*_PROFILING, I.E. FRAUD ASSESSMENT_*
{panel}

Another element that interests me is what signals/patterns do you have in mind here - do you perhaps have an RFC or a document outlining what signals we’d be taking into account in this case?

The reason why I am asking this is to understand if we’re not creating any space for discrimination or bias (e.g man+in his 30s+white = fraudster), as well as that we’re not engaging in profiling that would be harmful.

* our legal team was aware of this and so we cooperated from the early stage, with external advisor (Baker McKenzie) being closely involved in this as well
* all in all what was our understanding was that legal team is happy that we want to exclude branding bonus from the discount logic and treat it as a B2B service rendered from fleets to Bolt

We would also like to take this opportunity to clarify how location tracking operates within the Bolt Driver application. In particular, it is important to explain the technical distinction between the location permissions "Allow all the time" and "Allow while using the app":

* “Allow all the time” access means the application can track a Driver’s phone’s location as follows:
** When the Driver is *offline* (i.e., has explicitly set their status as offline to not provide the services): the location of the Driver is tracked only when the application screen is open.
** When the Driver is *online* (i.e., the Driver explicitly chose to set their status as online to provide the services): the location of the Driver is tracked when the application screen is open or the application is running in the background.
** In both scenarios, the Driver’s location is not tracked when the application is fully closed.
** For clarity, an application is considered to be “running in the background” when a Driver opens another application or returns to their phone’s home screen without closing the original application. In this state, the original application remains active and can perform tasks even though it is not currently visible on their screen.
* “While using the app” access means the application only tracks the Driver’s phone’s location when the application’s screen is open and the Driver is actively interacting with it. Once the Driver puts the application in the background, it stops receiving location updates. This access means the application can only access a Driver’s phone’s location when it’s visible on their screen. If the Driver switches to another application or the phone’s screen turns off, the application won’t receive location updates in the background.

To provide transportation services via Bolt Platform, Drivers are required to grant Bolt the permission to access their location data in "_Allow all the time_" mode. It is important to note that Bolt does not continuously track or access Driver location data 24/7 when "_Allow all the time_" permission is granted. This setting is essential to ensure the Bolt Driver Application functions properly when Drivers go online. It allows access to the Driver's location data both when the application screen is open and running in the background, enabling critical features such as accurate Passenger-Driver matching and real-time route optimization. These functions ensure that the Bolt Driver Application operates as intended and without interruptions, enabling seamless service provision to Passengers. 

*Purpose Limitation*

As outlined above, Drivers who want to provide transportation services via the Bolt Driver Application have to enable the "Allow all the time" location setting. This permission is essential to ensure the proper functioning of the critical features of the Bolt Driver Application.

As mentioned above, granting "Allow all the time" access by Drivers does not mean that Bolt continuously tracks or accesses location data at all times, in particular when the Driver is offline or the Bolt Driver Application is fully closed.

* On iOS, "Allow all the time" access permission is required by Bolt only when Drivers go online using the Bolt Driver Application. This permission ensures that the Driver's location data is collected whenever the Bolt Driver Application is open and running in the background while the Driver is online and providing services.
* The "Allow all the time" location permission is required for Android devices due to new policies and technical specifications introduced in Android 14. This update requires Bolt to ask Drivers to select the “Allow all the time” access permission to ensure that location data is collected whenever the Bolt Driver Application is open and running in the background while the Driver is online and providing services. This change was introduced through a software update to the Bolt Driver Application to align with these updated policies and ensure uninterrupted operation of the Bolt Driver Application. Despite this adjustment in how permissions are labeled, communicated to Drivers or managed on Android devices, the fundamental location tracking logic remains unchanged. Bolt continues to track Driver location only when they go online and the Bolt Driver Application is open or running in the background.

h3. 1. Translation and summary of the request

The document is a *Prosecutor’s Order* issued by the *District Prosecutor’s Office in Warsaw–Wola* (Prokuratura Rejonowa Warszawa–Wola) on *5 November 2025*, signed by *Assessor Karolina Dębowska*.

*Legal basis cited:* Article 180 §1 of the Polish Code of Criminal Procedure (Kodeks postępowania karnego, “k.p.k.”).

*Case reference:* 4316-1.Ds.515.2025
*Criminal offence:* Article 197 §2 of the Polish Criminal Code (rape).

*Request:*
The prosecutor orders *Bolt Polska Sp. z o.o.* to disclose personal data related to a *driver using a red Toyota Corolla, registration WPR6615T*, operating under the Bolt platform between *27 June 2025 (20:00)* and *28 June 2025 (08:00)*.
Requested data include:
a) all personal and contact details of the driver, and other related data;
b) full GPS route data, ride details, and passenger contact data during that time frame;
c) confirmation whether the driver’s account was active and used after 28 June 2025.

The order sets a *3-day deadline* from receipt for providing the data.

----

h3. 2. Legal basis analysis

The cited *Article 180 §1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure* is *not an accepted legal basis* according to Bolt’s internal list of legal bases.
However, Poland’s *Code of Criminal Procedure (k.p.k.)* contains other valid provisions that empower prosecutors to request data during criminal investigations, such as:

* *Article 218 §1 k.p.k.* – allows the prosecutor or court to require disclosure of correspondence and data, including electronic communications, from service providers;
* *Article 217 §1 and §236a k.p.k.* – allow seizure and production of digital evidence.

Article 180 §1 k.p.k. instead governs the *right of witnesses to refuse to testify when bound by professional secrecy*, and does *not* serve as a disclosure obligation for data controllers. Therefore, the cited basis is *invalid for compelling Bolt to disclose data*.

----

h3. 3. Proportionality and scope

The request concerns a *serious criminal offence (rape)* and is *limited in time (12 hours)* and *specific to a single driver and ride*. The data requested (driver identification, contact details, GPS logs, trip route, and passenger contact) are *relevant and proportionate* to the investigation.
Thus, *scope and proportionality are acceptable* provided a valid legal basis is invoked.

----

h3. 4. Recommendation to Risk & Compliance

The *legal basis (Art. 180 §1 k.p.k.) is invalid*, so *data cannot be disclosed as-is*.
Action steps:

# *Reject the request* in its current form.
# *Ask the Prosecutor’s Office to reissue the order* referencing a correct provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure, e.g. *Art. 218 §1* or *Art. 217 §1*, which authorise prosecutors to obtain data for criminal investigations.
# Once a corrected order is received, the request can be approved, and data disclosure limited to:
#* driver identification and contact details,
#* GPS and trip route data for 27–28 June 2025,
#* passenger identification limited to the relevant trip(s).

----

*Decision:* Deny until corrected.
*Instruction to CS:* Respond using the _“invalid legal basis – prosecutor order”_ template, explaining that Art. 180 §1 k.p.k. does not authorise data disclosure and that Bolt can only act upon a lawful order under the appropriate article of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The issue seems to be related to refund retries via cron job.

When the first refund fails the retries hit the Silverflow API with same idempotency-key but with different request body.

The problematic parameter is the {{reference}} key.

According to Silverflow if we’re retrying the request with the same idempotency-key the body has to be exactly same. This condition is validated on Silverflow side and is broken upon retries.

More details here: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06CX5FBSQ3/p1762431406607249|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06CX5FBSQ3/p1762431406607249|smart-link]

Bolt nije stranka u ugovoru o prijevozu, niti pružatelj takve usluge.

Također ističemo da je odgovornost za osobne predmete koje korisnici ostave u vozilu regulirana člankom 6.5 istih Općih uvjeta, koji jasno navodi kako Bolt ne snosi odgovornost za gubitak osobnih stvari, izravnu ili neizravnu materijalnu štetu, novčane iznose ili imovinske zahtjeve koji bi mogli proizaći iz korištenja aplikacije.

Uvidom u dostupne zapise potvrđeno je da je vozač čekao na dogovorenoj lokaciji više od 7 minuta te pokušao uspostaviti kontakt putem poziva i poruka. Budući da nije uspio stupiti u kontakt s Vama, sukladno članku 4.5 uvjeta, vozač je bio ovlašten otkazati vožnju, što je zabilježeno i u sustavu. Sukladno čl. 4.6, za takve slučajeve moguće je terećenje naknade za djelomično izvršenu uslugu i vrijeme čekanja.

S obzirom na ozbiljnost Vaših navoda, želimo Vas još jednom potaknuti da se – ukoliko smatrate da postoji osnovana sumnja na počinjenje kaznenog djela – obratite nadležnim tijelima, primjerice Ministarstvu unutarnjih poslova ili Državnom odvjetništvu. U slučaju službenog upita od strane ovlaštenih tijela, Bolt će, sukladno svojim zakonskim obvezama, u potpunosti surađivati i staviti na raspolaganje sve relevantne podatke koji su na raspolaganju, u skladu s propisima o zaštiti osobnih podataka.

Zahvaljujemo Vam na razumijevanju i stojimo na raspolaganju za eventualna dodatna pojašnjenja.

Thanks for flagging this. I’ve reviewed the letter n and can confirm the following:

* *The classification under the Digital Services Act (DSA)* - Ride-hailing platforms like Bolt generally fall within the DSA’s scope as intermediary services, more specifically online platforms under Article 3(i) DSA. This is because the app connects users with independent drivers, facilitating a commercial transaction between them.
* *However, the entity listed is incorrect.* The platform and related services in Ireland are provided by Bolt Operations OÜ (Estonia), not Bolt ITX Limited. Bolt ITX acts only as a local support and administrative entity and does not operate or provide the intermediary service itself.
* We suggest responding and request a correction, clarifying that Bolt ITX Limited should not be listed as the service provider. The competent Digital Services Coordinator for the Bolt platform should be the Estonian authority, not the Irish regulator. 
* Same for the the reference to a potential regulatory levy - it should not apply to Bolt ITX Limited once the record is corrected, as only the entity providing the intermediary service can be subject to such a levy.

Hi team, 

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 57.59 PLN, but order price was just 9.5 PLN (cancellation fee). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 48.09 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 9.5 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 57.59 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 9.5 PLN. 

57.59 PLN - 9.5 PLN = 48.09 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 48.09 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Let me know if you have any questions. 

Please note that this has been escalated to payment engineers to fix here. 
[https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PC-4376|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PC-4376?focusedCommentId=3408680&sourceType=mention]

Cheers, 
Marten

Hi team, 

I completely agree, the pages are a mess and its not very intuitive to understand what happened. 

Customer had an order for 18.61 PLN, Bolt negative bolt balance of 3.62 PLN from 25/07/2025, 08:30. 
We weren’t able to capture the full amount. 
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3523937795|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3523937795]

Customer had an order for 10 PLN + 3.62 PLN (13.62 PLN) on 03/11/2025, 11:58. Looks all good. 
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3523937795|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3523937795]

Customer had an order for 29.26 PLN on 04/11/2025, 11:33. Again Bolt was not able to capture the full amount and a negative balance was created for 0.62 PLN. 
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3822956757|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3822956757]

This explains the negative balance of 4.24 PLN. 

*So where does the negative balance of additional 7.26 PLN is coming from?* 

The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 20.88 PLN, but order price was just 13.62 PLN (cancellation fee + previous negative balance). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 7.26 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 13.62 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 20.88 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 13.62 PLN. 

20.88 PLN - 13.62 PLN = 7.26 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 7.26 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Let me know if you have any questions. 

Please note that this has been escalated to payment engineers to fix here.

Before moving forward, let's check if these are the events you want to track:

* GetObject / GetObjectVersion / SelectObjectContent → download/read
* CopyObject / UploadPartCopy (multipart copy) → copy/write
* PutObject → if someone copies data into your bucket

To capture these kinds of data events, you’ll need to enable CloudTrail with S3 data event logging. Keep in mind that CloudTrail data events can be quite costly, as they are billed per 100,000 events.

The second consideration is your requirement for alerts (“We would like to get alerts…”). This will need more than just enabling CloudTrail, you’ll need a setup that connects CloudTrail → EventBridge → SNS → Slack.

I’ve summarized below the outcomes of our Wednesday meeting.

*Agreed:*

* To implement multiple asset books.
* The reporting team confirmed that forex risk for assets sold intercompany, which continue to be accounted for in a currency other than EUR, is acceptable.
* The current Local GAAP asset book will be considered the *Statutory book*, since it currently reflects statutory accounting policies rather than Group policies. A separate book will be created for *Group asset accounting*.
* All assets for all companies will be copied by the end of 2025.
* During the copying process:
** All assets with a spend category other than _Micromobility_ will be copied to the Group book with the same accounting treatment and data as currently reflected in the Local GAAP (Statutory) book.
** _Micromobility_ assets that were sold or transferred intercompany will be registered in the Group book showing their *historical total cost* and *historical accumulated depreciation*.
** The *useful life* of such assets should be adjusted so that the life in the initial entity plus the useful life in the new entity equals the original useful life defined when the asset was first registered. This ensures that the periodic depreciation expense remains unchanged after an intercompany sale or transfer.
* For all future intercompany asset sales or transfers, assets should be recognized in the Group book of the new entity showing their *historical total cost* and *historical accumulated depreciation* (not NBV).

*I would suggest following Next Steps to Implement Multiple Books and Copy Assets:*

* Clearly define Statutory and Group asset books rules. The current Local GAAP asset book mixes statutory and group accounting principles and estimates.
* *Appoint a dedicated accountant* to support the copying and testing of assets of spend categories other than Micromobility. It is assumed that [~accountid:639b20bdf78d12c0f471a5e4]  will be responsible for copying and registering Micromobility items only.

    cd.duration,
    cd.search_category_group_name,
    cd.user_note,
    cd.claim_id
  --bu.group_name,
  --bu.external_user_id
  from
    business_details bd
      left join ng_public_spark.etl_business_rh_orders_core oc
        on oc.id = bd.order_id
        and oc.city_id = bd.city_id
        and oc.state in ('finished', 'client_did_not_show', 'client_cancelled')
        and oc.business_company_id = 49453
        and oc.order_created_local_date >= DATE('2025-08-01')
        and oc.order_created_local_date < DATE('2025-11-15')
      left join ng_commerce_billing_spark.etl_billing_invoicing_rides_user etl
        on etl.order_id = bd.order_id
        and etl.city_id = bd.city_id
        and etl.invoice_type = case
          when bd.transaction_type = 'claim' then 'invoice'
          else 'credit_note'
        end
        and etl.created_date >= DATE('2025-08-01')
        and etl.created_date < DATE('2025-11-15')
      left join ng_public_spark.business_invoicing_claim_data cd
        on cd.driver_id = case
          when etl.from_agent_type = 'ride_hailing_driver' then etl.from_agent_id
          else etl.from_agent_sub_id
        end
        and cd.order_system_order_id
        = etl.order_id--left join ng_public_spark.etl_business_business_user bu on bu.user_id = etl.to_user_id

),
order_metrics as (
  select
    order_id,
    city_id,
    array_agg(address) as destinations,
    count(*) as number_of_destinations
  from
    ng_public_spark.company_order_stop
  where
    type != 'pickup'
    and created_date >= DATE('2025-08-01')
    and created_date < DATE('2025-11-15')
  group by
    1,
    2
),
business_union as (
  select
    bm.*,
    om.destinations,
    om.number_of_destinations
  from
    business_metrics bm
      left join order_metrics om
        on om.order_id = bm.order_id
        and om.city_id = bm.city_id
),
pii_info as (
  select
    bu.*,
    concat(cd.business_user_first_name, ' ', cd.business_user_last_name) as user_name,
    '' as user_phone,
    cd.business_user_external_id as external_user_id,
    ug.name as group_name,
    c.uuid as ride_id
  from
    business_union bu
      left join ng_public_spark.business_invoicing_claim c
        on c.id = bu.claim_id
      left join ng_public_spark.business_invoicing_claim_data cd
        on cd.claim_id = bu.claim_id
      left join ng_public_spark.business_business_user_group ug
        on ug.id = c.business_group_id
)
select distinct
  balance_local_ts as date,
  ride_id,
  invoice_number,
  driver_name as service_provider_name,
  from_address as from,
  to_address as to,
  number_of_destinations,
  destinations,
  asc2.name as city,
  distance_in_km,
  duration as duration_in_minutes,
  search_category_group_name as vehicle_category_group,
  user_name,
  user_phone,
  case
    when transaction_type = 'claim' then 'ride'
    else 'refund'
  end as type,
  original_price,
  original_price
  - case
    when transaction_type = 'claim' then business_company_amount
    else original_price
  end as discount,
  round(
    (
      original_price
      - case
        when transaction_type = 'claim' then business_company_amount
        else original_price
      end
    )
    / original_price,
    2
  )
  * 100 as discount_percent,
  case
    when transaction_type != 'claim' then -business_company_amount
    else null
  end as refund_amount,
  case
    when transaction_type = 'claim' then business_company_amount
    else -business_company_amount
  end as total_cost_of_ride,
  group_name as user_group,
  external_user_id as employee_id,
  user_note as trip_reason,
  concat('https://claim.bolt.eu/?s=', ride_id) as invoice
from
  pii_info pi
    left join ng_public_spark.admin_system_city asc2
      on asc2.id = pi.city_id
order by date desc{noformat}

Coupon amount: 2.5 euro

Our system rounds this amount to the 0.12, and since there’re a lot of such Coupons, minor discrepancy persists.

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 40.43 PLN, but order price was just 9.5 PLN (cancellation fee). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 30.93 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 9.5 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 40.43 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 9.5 PLN. 

40.43 PLN - 9.5 PLN = 30.93 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 30.93 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Please let me know if you have any questions.

+*Clause 3.2 – Indemnity*+
We’ve retained the indemnity, as it’s essential to protect Bolt from losses caused by misuse or legal breaches. However, we’ve added concessions to make it more acceptable to the customer — limiting it to direct losses and capping liability at 12 months of fees. This keeps our protection intact but eases their internal approval concerns.

+*Clause 6.5 – Brand Use*+
The customer wanted assurance that Bolt can’t use their name or logo without explicit permission. We’ve clarified this by requiring *prior written consent* in each instance. It’s consistent with our current practice and poses minimal operational impact.

+*Clause 8.2 – Changes to Terms*+
We’ve kept Bolt’s ability to make unilateral updates (critical for managing terms across all customers) but added a *“material change” carve-out*. This means only significant updates affecting customer rights will require formal written agreement.

Overall, these updates maintain Bolt’s contractual flexibility and legal protection while demonstrating good faith in addressing the customer’s key sensitivities.

If the method you mentioned allows participants to leave the campaign only by unsubscribing from all communications from Bolt, it could be on my side acceptable — however, I don’t think it’s a good approach for Bolt itself. This is because in that case, a FO/driver would not only opt out of this particular campaign but also stop receiving future communications and opportunities to participate in similar initiatives.

Therefore, if by clicking the provided option users can leave the campaign itself - not just all comms - this approach works for me, considering the urgency in this matter.

Also, the *notification sent to FOs/drivers about opting out of this campaign must clearly state that by doing so, they will stop receiving all communications.* I should also mention, that this could lead to dissatisfaction among FOs/drivers and appear as a form of coercion — as if “if you don’t want to join this campaign, Bolt punishes you by cutting off all comms.”

As I understand, this is not the first campaign in Bolt’s history, so opt-out methods and functionality must have been used before. Perhaps it would be useful to consult with colleagues to see how this was previously handled to ensure full compliance while avoiding  FOs/driver frustration?

Hey [~accountid:5e4cfe3b393ea90c94b40eb0] thanks for reaching out.
Yes, we already have sustainable controls in place. We apply upper caps for all cancellations, and in some cases (like Port Harcourt), tighter thresholds for new users. Typically, we set limits on how many cancellations a rider can make within a 24-hour period. Once they exceed this threshold, their account is temporarily blocked.

Currently, for Port Harcourt, the rule for new users is that after 5 cancellations, the next one triggers a 1-hour block, with a prior warning shown to the rider.

We can certainly adjust these thresholds to be stricter during the protest period (typically a 1-day block + smaller cancellation limit + maybe consider past order activity) and later relax them once activity normalises. In doing so, we can take into account datapoints such as user age, total cancellations, no-show order counts etc.

As for who can make these changes, I’d recommend keeping this within the Fraud team. Fraud OPS have sufficient capacity to support protest-specific and general rule adjustments when needed. If you’d still prefer for your team to be able to modify these directly, it might be worth checking again with Aleksei in the initial thread, but in practice, Fraud has always handled this efficiently.

Since we don’t yet have a confirmed protest timeframe, I can do a quick analysis and pull suggested rider blocking thresholds based on past data, so we can align on a plan in advance.
Let me know your thoughts on this 🙂

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Marten

h2. ⚖️ *Executive Summary*

*Overall assessment:* ❌ _Partner’s template deviates materially from Bolt’s approved contracting model._
*Recommendation:* Reject use of partner’s template and propose execution via Bolt’s Special Terms (localized for Paraguay).

*Key findings:*

# ⚠️ *Mischaracterization of Bolt’s role* — defines Bolt Services PY S.A. as a “service provider” rather than digital intermediary; omits reference to _Bolt Operations OÜ_ as contracting party.
# ⚠️ *Local contracting entity risk* — use of _Bolt Services PY S.A._ contradicts global legal structure (Bolt Operations OÜ is the contracting entity; local entities act only as tax/collection agents).
# ⚠️ *Missing agency clause (commercial agent exemption)* — creates payment license and liability exposure.
# ⚠️ *Liability clause incomplete* — no limitation of liability or exclusion for driver/third-party acts (unlike approved clause 6.2–6.3.6 in playbook).
# ⚠️ *Confidentiality clause* — indefinite duration and “solidary liability” for breach → exceeds industry standard.
# ✅ *Correct role independence statement* (clause 6) — confirms no employment or joint venture; aligns with Bolt playbook.
# ⚠️ *Governing law/jurisdiction* — Paraguay law and Asunción courts; acceptable if only for local collection, but inconsistent with Bolt’s Estonia-based structure.
# ⚠️ *Data protection* — absent; no controller–controller reference or cross-reference to Bolt’s Privacy Notice.
# ✅ *Termination rights* — mutual and flexible (5 days); consistent with standard 7-day mutual termination but still acceptable.
# ⚠️ *Audit / access rights* — none now, but confidentiality and data gaps could indirectly permit overreach.

----

h2. 📊 *Detailed Clause Analysis*

||Topic||Clause Ref.||Risk Level||Analysis & Rationale||
|*Bolt Role & Entity Definition*|Cover page, cl. 2|*High*|Identifies _Bolt Services PY S.A._ as “Empresa” providing the platform and invoicing services. This conflicts with Bolt’s global model where _Bolt Operations OÜ_ is the contracting entity and local subsidiaries act as agents. Needs correction to preserve intermediary status and avoid carrier/tax registration risk.|
|*Scope of Services (Object)*|Cl. 2|*Medium–High*|Describes provision of “servicio de transporte privado de personas y envíos” — implies Bolt provides transport. Should be reframed as _digital platform enabling Users to connect with independent Drivers_.|
|*Agency / Payment Collection*|Cl. 4–5|*High*|Lacks “commercial agent” clause (equivalent to 3.7 of playbook). Without it, payments received by Bolt PY may be treated as own revenue, exposing to financial regulation. Must add agency language per approved wording.|
|*Liability*|Cl. 7|*High*|States limited disclaimer (“Empresa no se responsabilizará… por el servicio de los Conductores”), but omits liability cap and exclusions for indirect, consequential, or economic losses. Should follow playbook clause 6.1–6.3.6.|
|*Indemnity*|—|*Medium*|No express indemnity, but “solidary responsibility” in confidentiality (cl. 8.3) could function as one. Overbroad and not reciprocal.|
|*Audit / Access*|—|*Low*|No direct audit right – ✓ acceptable.|
|*Data Protection*|—|*High*|Entirely missing controller–controller language. Must add playbook 4.1 clause confirming each party acts as independent controller.|
|*Confidentiality*|Cl. 8|*Medium–High*|Obligations indefinite; “solidary liability” excessive vs. 5-year retention limit in Bolt template. Should mirror playbook clause 5.|
|*Use of Logo / Brand*|Cl. 6.5|*Low*|Restricts Bolt’s use of customer’s logo, but silent on customer use of Bolt’s. Add standard reciprocal restriction per 6.5.|
|*Termination*|Cl. 10|*Low–Medium*|5 days’ notice OK; aligns with playbook 7.2 flexibility (7 days). Should clarify survival of confidentiality and payment obligations.|
|*Jurisdiction & Law*|Cl. 16|*Medium*|Sets Paraguayan law & Asunción courts. Acceptable for local use _only if_ Bolt Operations OÜ not replaced as contracting entity. Otherwise, inconsistent with Estonia-governed model.|

----

h2. 🛠️ *Redline Proposals (Key Edits)*

*Before:* “La Empresa prestará el servicio de transporte privado de personas…”
*After:* “Bolt Operations OÜ, actuando como intermediario digital, pone a disposición una plataforma tecnológica que permite a los Usuarios conectar con Conductores independientes que ofrecen servicios de transporte privado.”
*Why:* Aligns with Bolt’s defined platform-intermediary role.

*Before:* “La Empresa emitirá una factura a crédito…”
*After:* “Bolt Operations OÜ, a través de su agente local Bolt Services PY S.A., emitirá la factura correspondiente como agente comercial autorizado.”
*Why:* Reinstates commercial agent structure required by clause 3.7 of playbook.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

So what happens with these cases is other party will send legal letters, we generally reply, but ultimately, if they are to proceed, it gets referred to the Personal Injuries Board in Ireland (this preceeds any potential civil court action). They will then contact us and in the past, we have said, no, we are not at fault, and then the claimant will have to take a legal case (most, if not all don't proceed past this point due to costs).

Attaching some further logs, our system in place is;

# User reports an accident to Customer Service
# Customer Service takes the scooter offline (no one else can hire)
# A vehicle collect task is automatically assigned
# Local team collects the scooter and brings it back to depot
# Automatic safety check is activated
# Local team has to assess via our mechanics app and the vehicle has to pass the test before it can de deployed on the street again



Time line of events for this case;

# Customer contacted Bolt at 17:53 on 10/04
# Bolt responded at 17:54 on 10/04 as the customer mentioned an ambulance
# Bolt attempted to call the customer at 18:07 on 10/04, as no answer via in-app message
# Scooter was taken offline, and Collect task was assigned at 18:24 on 10/04
# Scooter collected by the local team at 07:30 on 11/04
# Safety check opened in depot at 11:24 on 11/04
# No issues found with the scooter, safety check passed, and returned to operational mode at 18:41 on 11/04

Agree that MHC will add significant weight due to their size and presence in IE. Should the claimant continue to escalate after such, then I would let them go down the route of Personal Injuries Board (of which we will not agree to) and following which they will have to take a civil case (costly) to proceed any further. ** EOS were also adamant that, because their TOMs were up to standard, a DSA should not be necessary. I explained that the DSA is not just about TOMs, but instead is a means of: (i) ensuring accountability / data processing clarity; (ii) codifying compliance with requirements that should already apply to controllers; (iii) introducing obligations that are important to Bolt from an operational POV (e.g., notifying bolt about relevant personal data breaches); and (iv) introducing a specific indemnity for data protection violations. Unfortunately, EOS seemed hesitant to acknowledge any of these points.
** EOS also maintained that any amendments should be proposed through their ‘special T&Cs’ that they have been discussing with the wider team - this is partly why they have not accepted any of our amendments to date (I was not aware that this was the previously agreed form of suggesting amendments).
* Ultimately, it seems that EOS’s unwillingness to accept the DSA comes from: (1) a fundamental understanding of data protection requirements and of the DSA itself; and (2) an unwillingness to depart from their standard terms. As such, it seems extremely unlikely that they will accept a full DSA in any form.
** NB. Having googled the call participants (Lars-Oliver and Melanie), neither of them are lawyers, nor privacy specialists. They also tried to argue that implementing SCCs goes against data minimisation requirements under the GDPR, and so unfortunately I am not convinced that they are well versed on privacy matters. They are ultimately more interested in ‘getting the deal done’ and do not have much regard for privacy issues.
* As such, I proposed a middle ground - *I would delete the DSA in its entirety and draft 4 or 5 ‘light touch’ data sharing provisions* to be included in the special T&Cs, which cover the key points. This would eliminate EOS’s (arguably unfounded) concerns about joint controllership, and make the pill easier to swallow.
** EOS seemed open to this suggestion on the call, and proposed that I should send over the suggested provisions via email.
*** EOS noted that the indemnity might get some pushback (EOS failed to see how an EOS data breach could cause liability for Bolt - this was explained to EOS on the call, but unfortunately they did not seem to be receptive to it), but they would still be willing to see a draft.
** EOS flagged that I could also include previously discussed terms about SCD and international data transfers. 
*** NB. The SCD point is already included in the special T&Cs (see p.7 [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ry6C7-n7jlX0ayZ3Z19Yd29g8Cw7_xzV/edit]).
* NB. Lars-Oliver will be OOO next week, and so this will be covered by Melanie and Carolyn on the EOS side.

Hello [~accountid:5f6cafc5473df20070678b8f], thank you for waiting for my response 🙏 

Usually, a Code of Conduct contains broad, internationally recognised principles and expectations for ethical and environmental standards. However, in this case, what stands out are the _extensive audit rights_ granted to RCE.

RCE requires suppliers and their subcontractors to have internal systems that ensure compliance with its Code of Conduct. Each supplier must appoint a responsible contact person to oversee implementation, communicate requirements internally, and maintain documentation. RCE may at any time request evidence of compliance through audits, site visits, or written reports, and suppliers are also obliged to disclose full contact details of all subcontractors upon request.


I would _not recommend signing_ a Code of Conduct with audit clauses this broad. It gives RCE wide and unlimited inspection powers - including over subcontractors - without clear limits on scope, timing, or confidentiality. This creates significant administrative, commercial, and data protection risks for us. 

If you have any additional questions, please let me know, thanks!

Hey [@emelie.dufva|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U06T67GD6CU] - fun situation! My thoughts below - references to sections are to those in [current global terms template|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RVNXe1lW1DprrmpSnXUdty4r6PZ9V4qm8I6AoGmDinU/edit?tab=t.0], so you'll want to double check the applicable DK terms.

*Our obligations and choices*

* Bolt’s obligations depend on any transport regulatory duties that apply to it by law. Where such duties exist, Bolt must comply. Outside those cases, it is not Bolt’s role to intervene in the relationship between fleet owners and drivers.
* That said, Bolt may still choose to investigate suspected breaches of its terms (see section 11). Fleets remain responsible for preventing unlawful behaviour on the platform (section 10.1) and must not allow conduct that could significantly harm Bolt’s reputation (section 10.6.5). Bolt may suspend or terminate a fleet driver’s access — as part of the fleet’s overall access — where breaches occur (sections 12 and 13). This enables Bolt to address problematic fleet drivers.
* A fleet’s claim that a driver is “bad” is not, on its own, a valid reason to refuse re-registration. Bolt should be able to verify any problems independently, not rely on hearsay, if it's going to restrict access and prevent 're-registrations' with another fleet.

*Re-registering*

* Bolt reserves the right to refuse platform access to any fleet driver who has previously caused a fleet to be in breach of the terms (see section 6.4). The licence for a driver to access the platform continues only while there is no risk of damage to Bolt’s reputation (section 3.4.6). These provisions give Bolt sufficient discretion to prevent problem drivers from returning to the platform... assuming there is a documented ground for suspension that we can rely on for these purposes.
* In practice, details of any problem driver should be recorded so onboarding can be blocked if they attempt to re-register. The safety team likely already manages this for removed drivers. If not, that process should be established.

*Next steps and other considerations*

* If we want to take action, we need to find a breach of our terms that we will rely on to suspend access.
* If local operations want to prevent re-registrations, they should involve the safety team to identify how to stop that individual rejoining the platform. There should already be a process or flagging mechanism for this.
* Depending on licensing rules, the fleet (or Bolt) could also consider reporting the driver to the relevant regulatory body. Bolt can choose to do so as well, but any concerns should be well substantiated.
* Do check the DK terms for equivalent provisions (you may want to check if the situation involves a 4X27 driver).

I hope that helps!

If the same Bolt Rewards programme is planned in Denmark as in other nordic countries (including EV charging, discounts on spare parts, and discounts on car washes), I believe the programme can be considered permissible.

*So our goal shoul be to* offer neutral, low-value, third-party commercial perks that don’t *(i)* steer work behavior, *(ii)* look like pay or “benefits,” or *(iii)* deepen integration with Bolt.

# *Inclusivity first (lowest risk).*
#* *Default: open to all active drivers*, no thresholds. This avoids a “performance management” aura that implies control/integration (key misclassification triggers in Danish practice and the EU directive’s “direction & control” test).
# *If you need eligibility rules, use one neutral filter only.*
#* The only tolerable filter is *ride completion rate* (pure service quality proxy).
#* *Do not* use acceptance or cancellation rates; these are classic *control levers* and will be read against us—particularly in light of Danish sensitivity post-Wolt.[ |https://www.hk.dk/-/media/images/om-hk/sektorer/privat/hkprivat/pdf/2022/wolt_skatteraadets_afgoerelse.pdf?hash=23CA29F1E4E7CE3AA1584DAC3DA569E3&la=da]
# *Keep value small and clearly non-wage.*
#* *Hard caps* (e.g., monthly and annual) and *no cash equivalents*.
#* *No reimbursements* or wallet top-ups; *vendor-side discounts only* so there’s no resemblance to remuneration. That also preserves the Danish “own economic risk / substantial own costs” indicator for genuine self-employment.[ |https://info.skat.dk/data.aspx?oid=2048530&utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# *Make it third-party and portable.*
#* Structure as *supplier-run discounts* (EV charging networks, parts retailers, car-wash operators). Bolt only facilitates codes/links.
#* Where feasible, allow *non-Bolt professional drivers* to use the same public discount pages—this reduces “exclusive integration” with Bolt.
# *Strict neutrality in presentation.*
#* Call it *“Driver Supplier Discounts”* (not “loyalty” or “benefits”).
#* *Zero impact* on dispatch, price, access to trips, support tiers, or deactivation review queues—spell that out in the T&Cs and the app UI.
# *No branding obligations.*
#* *Never condition access* on wearing Bolt-branded clothing or using Bolt-branded tools. Social perception (uniforms/logos) is a listed risk factor in Denmark.[ |https://info.skat.dk/data.aspx?oid=2048530&utm_source=chatgpt.com]
# *Substitution and multi-homing protected.*
#* Rewards must *not* restrict drivers from using substitutes (where local licensing allows) or from working on other platforms. If any vendor requires named-person accounts, note explicitly that use of substitutes remains a driver choice.
# *Hands off “discipline.”*
#* Rewards must *not* reference deactivation, warnings, suspensions, or ratings. In Denmark, control via sanctions is high-salience evidence of an employment relationship (see Wolt file; and remember SIRI already treats Wolt as employer for EU worker registration).[ |https://www.hk.dk/-/media/images/om-hk/sektorer/privat/hkprivat/pdf/2022/wolt_skatteraadets_afgoerelse.pdf?hash=23CA29F1E4E7CE3AA1584DAC3DA569E3&la=da]
# *Data minimisation & transparency.*
#* Share only what’s needed to redeem a discount. No performance data flows to vendors. Future Danish transposition of the Platform Work Directive will heighten attention to platform-held data and automated decisions—don’t give anyone a reason to argue Rewards is part of algorithmic management

h3. *Red flags to avoid (these would be cited as “direction & control”)*

* Tiered *loyalty* (Silver/Gold/Platinum), streaks, or bonus ladders tied to *acceptance/cancellation* or hours-online.
* *Priority dispatch* or queue jumps for Rewards users.
* *Cash-equivalent* perks (gift cards, wallet credits, reimbursements).
* *Exclusive* deals that require using Bolt logos, attending Bolt trainings, or keeping ratings/acceptance above set thresholds to remain eligible.
* Any *disciplinary link* (e.g., “loss of Rewards if your rating drops”).

Yes, compensating drivers for unpaid trips creates risk for Bolt, since it makes it difficult to explain why Bolt is taking on the financial risk of another “independent business.” To avoid driver reclassification, Bolt needs to be able to show that drivers bear their own financial risk.The markets you mention are sensitive, but the underlying issue is the same across all markets. You can find a breakdown of market sensitivities [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iRAIxZgCb9EAGtb6nPaPsRG4ExKL-OGSaYcFhz49SNc/edit?gid=0#gid=0] (simplified table). 

What makes a market riskier than another is essentially driver and regulator sentiment, which is independent of any specific feature or change Bolt introduces.We do need to strike a balance and consider user experience, so whether drivers are compensated or not is a call for central ops, with input from local teams.

The standing approach for Central Operations remains as per this [document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-1FZ72CsnSTczqrI-ZsJkYTUaE7udRW5ycDWsq1kfUY/edit?tab=t.0]:

# Preferred - do not compensate for unpaid trips
# Second option (if GM can justify) - compensate until a threshold - this demonstrates the driver still bears most of the financial responsibility and we only cover where necessary. Thresholds are uniformly applied given parameters - those are not subject to revision.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt plans to open x2 kiosks in Ukraine. We are currently in talks with Respublika Park Mall in Kyiv as a venue.
** Kiosk provider has not yet been selected, so no contract signed yet. Otherwise, no indication as to timeline.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* EU Assessment was done here: [+*LINK*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Hh2KUwVMeD2MqEzHa-UWF-IlqIyvLfPyO7mrkj3-V7c/edit?tab=t.0]. 
** This is in Ukraine, which is not in the EU. However, Ukraine has taken steps to harmonise local requirements with the GDPR (a Draft Law No. 8153, dated October 25, 2022, was submitted to the Parliament of Ukraine to harmonise the Data Protection Law with the provisions of the GDPR - However, due to war in Ukraine, GDPR not yet implemented there).
*** Ukraine law recognised an equivalent of legitimate interests, transparency obligations, controller-processor obligations and DSRs. See[^Law of Ukraine on Personal Data Protection 03 09 2015.pdf] 
*** EEA recognised as an adequate jurisdiction.
*** Consent required for direct marketing (or no consent needed if person can opt out).
** However, ‘Risky Data’ in Ukraine includes location and/or routes of movement of a person. Also, financial data (payment card / bank details) is considered sensitive.
* In terms of how this impacts the assessment:
** +Marketing+: Advice is the same ✅ 
*** We should ensure that marketing comms are disabled by default for passengers without a Bolt account.
** +Vendor data sharing+: Advice is the same ✅ 
*** We should implement a data processing agreement with the kiosk provider. From some brief research, it appears that the requirements regarding the contents of a DPA are less stringent under Ukrainian law - as such, our template DPA should be fine.
** +Transparency+: Advice is the same ✅ 
*** We should provide access to the full passenger privacy notice at all relevant times. Contents should be sufficient. 
*** However, Ukrainian law also requires us to disclose the *identity and location (ideally address) of any processors*. Since this will not be included in the privacy notice, we should consider explicitly identifying the kiosk provider during the order flow ⚠️ 
** +Unintended Disclosure+: Advice is the same ✅ 
*** We should take the proposed steps not to accidentally disclose driver or passenger data (including auto-clear screens and limited-time QR codes). This is particularly important since data subjects have an explicit right to data security under Ukrainian law.
** +Request responses+: Advice is the same ✅ 
*** We should ensure that CS is well-equipped to deal with requests.
** +Other+: Financial and location data are considered ‘risky’ under Ukrainian law. However, should not require any changes to the flow ✅ 
*** Ordinarily, the only additional requirement here is that they are notified to the regulator (since Bolt is processing this already, this should have already been done).
*** Therefore, more relevant requirements are taking greater steps to ensure security, transparency and minimisation controls. Technically, this makes legitimate interest a _weaker_ legal basis, but not invalid (i.e., even though these data categories are ‘risky’ they are not the equivalent of special category data - as such, we can rely on the same legal bases as usual).
*** NB. Technically, we are not processing payment details in all cases anyway - this may just be the kiosk provider. As such, we are more interested in location information.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Advise the business that we can roll this out, provided that: (i) the usual mitigations apply; plus (ii) we identify the kiosk provider by name and address during the order flow.

*Update 10 November 2025:*

* Investigated the causes of the difference between BA & Marketing dashboard which primarily can be attributed to the definition of new user and can be summarized as below:
** City status
*** BR report includes both active & inactive cities
*** Marketing report includes only include active cities --> this assumes the previously agreed signup logic
** City ID
*** BR report is based on city of order
*** Marketing report is based on user city ID in operating countries which is assumed to be based on city of signup based on the previous discussion with @/Balaji Senthilkumar.
* Proposed solution:
** Signup will not be altered. Signup count will still be counted after city launch date.
**  Activation will be counted:
*** Based on city of order (previously city of signup).
**** City ID of activated users in marketing report should be attributed to city of order to maintain data consistency. Caveat of this approach is that from perspective of user journey, it might be broken as order city is not necessarily the same with signup city.
*** Regardless of city launch date (will take both activations before and after city launch date).
**** City status in marketing report can be ignored while considering activation calculations—this assumes that user can only order if we have launched operation in that particular city. The caveat of this approach is that we have inconsistent logic between signup and new users and from the perspective of user journey, some users will have order without signup.
* [*Dashboard is now updated based on the latest logic*|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/28043].

*Update 10 November 2025*:

* [Dashboard RR logic|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/28043] is updated and is currently under validation. Last BR report did not have RR estimation as it reported full October actual. Therefore, the validation needs to be carried out by week 46-47 to be able to compare it with BR calculation.

This is a Partnership Agreement between Bolt Operations OÜ ("Bolt") and Stella Energy Norway AS ("Partner") for the Bolt Rewards Program in Norway. The agreement, effective October 20, 2025, outlines the terms for Stella to provide discounted EV charging services to Bolt Drivers and Fleet Owners.Key aspects of the agreement include:

* *Bolt Rewards Program*: Bolt will showcase Stella's offers (Tiered Discounts and a Special Onboarding Promotion) to Drivers and Fleet Owners via the Bolt App and Platform.
* *Stella's Commitments*: Stella will sell electricity through its charging network in Oslo, offer tiered pricing based on consumption (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Diamond tiers), and provide introductory benefits for new Fleet Owners. Stella will also share data on network usage and expansion plans.
* *Bolt's Commitments*: Bolt will promote Stella's offers, provide verified lists of eligible Drivers and Fleet Owners for onboarding, and share anonymized trip data to help Stella optimize its network.
* *Bolt Operator Reward Scheme (Appendix 1 - Annex 1)*: This scheme allows Bolt to earn free kilowatt-hour rewards based on aggregated Driver and Fleet Owner consumption on the Stella Network. These Reward Kilowatt Hours can then be allocated to Drivers or Fleet Owners by Bolt.

The agreement can be seen as a barter arrangement meaning that supplies should be taxed with VAT and reported as appropriate. As legal was unable to address the barter aspect and come to a conclusion or mitigation steps, some wording was suggested to the Appendix to highlight lack of reciprocity, but the risk remains.

Advise the customer to check with their bank to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to 30 days to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hi all, [~accountid:712020:79bdda29-2f20-4318-9d05-92c9d0bd7b47] , as discussed, I reviewed the A1, LAQO agreements in comparison to the proposed HNK agreement.

This really comes down to a legal question and I can only advise on the HNK agreement as currently drafted. Right now, the HNK agreement, as drafted, is a taxable exchange. As discussed, HNK would invoice for and owe VAT on the 16K (~3200), the value of the ad services, but would only receive 2500 in non-fungible rides credits from Bolt. The agreement is economically imbalanced, and could potentially be viewed as artificial by tax authorities, which would deny any VAT reclaim by Bolt.

How to make the HNK agreement non-taxable like A1/LAQO is a legal question. Legal team should be able to think through recharacterizing the agreement as a mutual cooperation instead of a sponsorship. I would consider removing the invoicing and valuation clauses and clarify the Bolt rides credits are for the public, not HNK’s own staff use (i.e., to bring patrons to the theatre, cultural purpose). The agreement should clearly state there is no compensation or consideration exchanged, like the A1/LAQO agreements. Finally, the agreement likely needs to say that each party bears its won costs and performs marketing activities voluntarily. In other words, the purpose of the contract is a joint outreach to cultural audiences; Bolt gives credits to HNK to bring people to the theatre, and separately, HNK distributes and displays Bolt discounts codes specifically for rides to and from the theatre. If drafted this way, there would be no taxable supply, no VAT, and no need for invoices.

Hi all! My 2 cents on how we've done B2G for the past 7 years in Bolt Business as far as I have visibility.
cc [~accountid:60d6dd5cc90cb20068954dfc] [~accountid:6151cf6878e5e40070fb74c2] 

* On a tender by tender basis per ad hoc local Sales initiative. Foremost in the Baltics, also in PT, occasionally elsewhere but picking up now (especially in CEE).
* With each tender we're jumping the same loops* as each tender comes with the similar control-heavy/ transportation services related requirements (SLAs, fixed pricing, etc) which do not align with our platform operator narrative. Requirements we shouldn't be committing to as long as we operate B2G via the b2c Rides infrastructure w/o any ringfence.

_*Jumping the same loops - Legal flags the risks, Rides (and sometimes PP) looped in where needed to confirm we're ready to accept the risk. In most cases it's decided to move ahead. Especially in Baltics it's more fast track due to longer practice and perceived lower risk (for now)._

* In each single tender I've been included to *it's Bolt who is the contracting party* towards the public buyer. 

So the current setup whereby _Bolt would be "borrowing its capacity to a 3rd party" who would be contracting the public buyer_ is novel for Bolt Business tendering initiatives.
What exact commitments we should or shouldn't be making in ES for the cases at hand I'd kindly rely on [~accountid:712020:1a3a17cb-2e37-4162-8d95-4d1059255d7e] 's advice considering the specifics of the case🙏

Hi [~accountid:712020:9bc1ca8e-c2f1-41a2-9476-90ce966c2205] , thanks for the follow-up, let me clarify so we stay fully aligned with the setup we already agreed on.

The *opt-in you’re currently running is correct and should stay in place*, as it’s aligned with our framework for third-party marketing under Bolt Rewards. What we should _not_ do is move this consent into the Terms & Conditions, as that would not meet the GDPR standard for valid consent. Consent can’t be implied or bundled into a service contract.

To address your specific questions:

* *No, we can’t skip the opt-in* or rely only on the in-app marketing consent for this purpose. The _third_party_marketing_ toggle in the Driver App remains the *single source of truth* for whether a driver agrees to partner marketing. The opt-in campaign is precisely how we collect that consent and ensure it’s reflected in that field.
* *Yes, you can update the driver’s preference* (the _third_party_marketing_ field) *based on your current opt-in campaign*, provided that each update corresponds to an explicit “yes” from the driver during the call or prompt. If the driver declines or doesn’t respond, the toggle should remain off.

The flow - ask for consent first, then record and proceed only if accepted - is compliant and we can continue to use it without adding any T&Cs clause.

Let me know if all is clear 🙂

Hi! This is related to any bonuses, deductions or compensations that are not part of the delivery fee paid by the client. You can refer to the 7. FEES and 8. INVOICING part of the T&C as to where this is determined. 

Essentially there are two flows:

# Invoices from courier to the eater (Bolt invoices the eater on courier’s behalf)
## 8.1. Bolt, acting as an agent of the Delivery Partner, shall prepare and issue to the Client or the Bolt Business Customer the invoice(s) for the Delivery Fee and (where applicable) for the Small Order Fee and the Tips on behalf of the Delivery Partner and accept the Client’s orBolt Business Customer’s payment for the invoice(s) on behalf of the Delivery Partner, except for cash payment.
# If the actual earnings (explained int he FEES section) differ from the amount the client paid, Bolt will adjust the earnings accordingly and generate the appropriate invoice
## in the current case, the courier has received a bonus (meaning the actual earnings were bigger than what the eater paid, so Bolt compensated that part → can happen e.g when there’s a discount of something for the eater) and also a compensation for a long wait at a restaurant.
## The current invoice is generated from courier to Bolt, meaning that Bolt is responsible for paying this to the provider as part of the weekly payout
# Total payout = invoices from courier to eater + invoice for any marketplace fees applied (in this case a bonus and a waiting time compensation).
